pages.markdown:
# Repository availability contracts

A repository availability contract states how many verified copies, operators,
and regions hold a repository, which transports and refs they serve, how often
that is checked, how fast incidents are answered, and what is credited on a
miss. Each period yields a `forkmesh-availability-contract-report-v1` report
computed only from an evidence bundle, so anyone can recompute and verify it.
Managed checkout stays disabled until the [business model](business-model.md)
gates pass.

## Evidence bundle

Schema `forkmesh-availability-contract-evidence-v1`: `contract` (terms,
remedies, exclusions, fee), `observations` (`/api/repo/<owner>/<repo>/mirrors`
payloads, scored by the [availability proof](availability-proof.md)), `drills`
(restore drill records), `responses` (incident acknowledgements), and
`capacity` (`community` or `contracted` per node).

## Contract terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `copies` | Verified copies required in every slot. |
| `operators` | Distinct operators holding the same verified state (at least 2). |
| `regions` | Distinct regions among verified copies. |
| `uptimeBps` | Share of slots that must meet every check. |
| `verificationIntervalMs` | Slot length; at most 10,000 slots per period. |
| `transports` | `router`, `directHttps`, `smartHttp`, each needing a verified copy. |
| `refCoverage` | Copies must carry every branch. |
| `artifactCoverage` | Copies must carry every release artifact. |
| `recoveryTimeObjectiveMs` | Longest incident and slowest restore drill allowed. |
| `drillIntervalMs` | Oldest allowed drill at period end. |
| `incidentResponseMs` | Longest time to acknowledge an incident. |
| `failureTolerance` | Operators, and separately regions, that may fail at once (0 to 2). |
| `maxExcludedBps` | Share of slots exclusions may remove. |

Malformed terms stop evaluation with a closed error code; there is no partial
report.

## Verification slots

A slot misses on any failed check; a slot without evidence is a miss.

| Check | The slot misses when |
| --- | --- |
| `unverified` | No observation. |
| `quorum_below_contract` | Too few operators held the same verified state. |
| `copies_below_contract` | Too few verified copies. |
| `regions_below_contract` | Too few regions. |
| `transport_missing` | A contracted transport had no verified copy. |
| `ref_coverage_incomplete` | Too few copies carried every branch. |
| `artifact_coverage_incomplete` | Too few copies carried every artifact. |

Availability is `met slots * 10000 // counted slots`, rounding in the
customer's favor.

## Exclusions

Kinds `scheduled-maintenance`, `customer-requested`, and `legal-hold` remove
whole slots when announced before they start and within `maxExcludedBps`.
Rejections: `unknown_kind`, `announced_late`, `over_budget`.

## Incidents and drills

Consecutive missed slots form one incident, measured in whole slots. Response
states: `ok`, `late`, `missing`, `pending`. The latest restore drill per node
decides its state: `ok`, `drill_missing`, `drill_stale`,
`drill_beyond_objective`. See
[node backup and recovery](operations/node-backup-and-recovery.md).

## SLOs and remedies

SLOs: `availability`, `recovery`, `incident-response`, `restore-drills`. The
period is `met` only when all four are met. Every miss is listed, even when its
SLO holds:

| Miss | SLO |
| --- | --- |
| `availability_window` | `availability` |
| `recovery_objective_exceeded` | `recovery` |
| `response_late` | `incident-response` |
| `response_missing` | `incident-response` |
| `drill_missing` | `restore-drills` |
| `drill_stale` | `restore-drills` |
| `drill_beyond_objective` | `restore-drills` |

Credits come from `remedies`: one `availabilityTiers` credit for missed
availability, fixed credits per recovery, response, and drill miss, capped at
`maxCreditBps`. Money is integer micro-USD.

## Demonstrated capacity and admission

A node is demonstrated when it verified in at least `uptimeBps` of slots and
its latest drill is `ok`. Undeclared capacity counts as community. A contract
is admissible only when demonstrated capacity meets the terms; otherwise
`admission.reasons` lists `no_evidence`, `copies_not_demonstrated`,
`operators_not_demonstrated`, `regions_not_demonstrated`, or
`failure_simulation_failed`.

The failure simulation removes every combination of `failureTolerance`
operators, then regions, from the latest observation and recomputes the
quorum; a surviving node's drill must fit the recovery objective.

## Correlated-risk disclosures

Disclosures do not change the outcome.

### `community_capacity_relied_on`

Contracted capacity alone does not reach the operator quorum.

### `contracted_single_operator`

One operator runs every contracted copy.

### `operator_concentration`

One operator runs more than half of the demonstrated copies.

### `region_concentration`

More than half of the demonstrated copies share one region or none.

### `no_failure_headroom`

Losing any one operator breaks the quorum.

### `capacity_not_demonstrated`

A declared contracted node lacks continuous probes or a qualifying drill.

## Privacy

Reports show opaque operator numbers only, never accounts, endpoints, mirror
URLs, drill paths, or keys.

## Signed reports and tooling

A `forkmesh-availability-contract-signed-report-v1` document holds `report`,
`reportHash` (`sha256:` over canonical JSON), and an Ed25519 signature over
`forkmesh-availability-contract-report-v1\n<reportHash>`.

```sh
tools/forkmesh_availability_contract.py explain bundle.json
tools/forkmesh_availability_contract.py sign bundle.json --private-key seed.txt > signed.json
tools/forkmesh_availability_contract.py verify bundle.json signed.json --public-key <key>
tools/forkmesh_availability_contract.py fixture
```

`verify` recomputes the report and rejects edits to the report or evidence.
Exit codes: `explain` 0 met, 3 otherwise; `verify`/`fixture` 0 match, 1
mismatch; 2 for bad input. Model and fixture live in
`conformance/availability-contract/v1/`; tests in
`app/tests/test_availability_contract.py`. Reports are produced offline; drill
records are not signed.

pages.title: Availability proof and repository risk
pages.description: The forkmesh-availability-proof-v1 report says whether a repository is preserved, how independently, and what is at risk. It is computed from the public mirrors payload, so…
pages.markdown:
# Availability proof and repository risk

The `forkmesh-availability-proof-v1` report says whether a repository is
preserved, how independently, and what is at risk. It is computed from the
public mirrors payload, so anyone can recompute it.

## Evidence

Inputs come only from `GET /api/repo/<owner>/<repo>/mirrors`: signed endpoint
receipts (`endpointFresh`, `endpointHealthy`, `endpointIntegrity`,
`checkedAt`), direct clone probes (`directVerified`, `directCheckedAt`,
`directRefsSha256`), integrity gate verdicts (`integrity`, `behind`, `status`,
`lastSeen`), operator and region, and coverage (`branchCount`,
`artifactCount`). A receipt counts for 10 minutes; a passing probe for 24 hours.

## Copy classes and quorum

Each copy gets the first matching class: `failing`, `verified`, `declared`,
`stale`, `observed`. Reason codes: `integrity_rejected`, `abuse_blocked`,
`probe_failed`, `offline`, `behind`, `evidence_expired`, `awaiting_receipt`,
`never_observed`, `limited_replica`. A copy whose `replicaScope` is not `full`
is `observed` with `limited_replica` (see [Offline and low-bandwidth
sync](offline-sync.md)) and never counts toward quorum.

Proof is `quorum` when at least 2 distinct operators hold the same verified
state, `partial` with any verified copy, otherwise `none`. When probe digests
disagree, only the digest backed by the most operators counts. The risk score
is the sum of applicable weights, capped at 100: `critical` from 60, `high`
from 30, `moderate` from 10, else `low`.

## Risk codes

### `no_verified_copy`
Weight 50, critical. No copy has fresh signed evidence. **Remediation:** ask a node to mirror the repository, or [run a mirror node](operations/).

### `quorum_not_met`
Weight 25, high. Fewer than 2 operators hold the same verified state. **Remediation:** ask another operator to mirror it.

### `state_disagreement`
Weight 20, high. Verified copies returned different refs digests. **Remediation:** rerun the direct URL check; a divergent mirror re-syncs.

### `single_operator`
Weight 10, medium. All verified copies share one operator. **Remediation:** ask a different operator to mirror it.

### `failing_copy`
Weight 10, medium. A copy failed integrity, abuse checks or its clone probe. **Remediation:** re-sync the mirror and recheck it.

### `source_offline`
Weight 10, medium. The working-copy source is offline. **Remediation:** start the node that holds the working copy.

### `no_direct_clone_url`
Weight 10, medium. No verified copy passed a direct clone probe in 24 hours. **Remediation:** register a direct mirror URL and check it.

### `partial_ref_coverage`
Weight 10, medium. Too few verified copies carry every branch. **Remediation:** re-sync every branch.

### `stale_copy`
Weight 5, low. A copy is offline, behind or expired. **Remediation:** bring it back online.

### `partial_artifact_coverage`
Weight 5, low. Too few verified copies carry every release artifact. **Remediation:** re-sync release artifacts.

### `single_region`
Weight 5, low. All verified copies declare the same region. **Remediation:** ask a node in another region to mirror it.

### `declared_only_copy`
Weight 3, low. A catalog record exists but nothing has observed it. **Remediation:** check the endpoint is registered and reachable.

## Privacy and tooling

Operators appear only as opaque numbers; endpoint addresses and probe reasons
are never shown. The report is the `availability` field of the mirrors API
(`app/src/availability_proof.py`). `tools/forkmesh_availability_proof.py
verify|explain|fixture` recomputes it. The model and fixture live in
`conformance/availability-proof/v1/`.

pages.markdown:
# Back up a GitHub repository

This guide is for keeping a private, safe copy of a repository that lives on
GitHub, for example a website you share with a friend, without changing
anything on GitHub. You need two commands in a terminal; everything else
happens in the ForkMesh desktop app.

## What you need first

- **Permission to view the repository on GitHub.** If you can open its files
  on github.com, that is enough. You do not need permission to push, and you
  do not need a new branch: a backup only reads.
- **A ForkMesh account** and the desktop app, signed in. See
  [Getting started](getting-started.md); the desktop uses the same email and
  password as the website.
- **Git** on your computer. On Debian or Ubuntu: `sudo apt install git`.

## The words, in plain terms

| Word | What it means | Does it change GitHub? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| View | Look at the files on github.com | No |
| Clone | Make a copy of the repository on your computer | No |
| Pull | Bring the newest changes from GitHub into that copy | No |
| Commit | Save a change you made, on your computer only | No |
| Push | Send your saved changes to GitHub | **Yes**, and it can change the live website |
| Mirror | ForkMesh's copy of a repository, kept on the ForkMesh network | No |

A backup uses only **clone** and **pull**. ForkMesh never pushes anything to
GitHub for you.

On the ForkMesh website, **Import from GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg** copies a
project's issues and pull requests once. It does not copy the code and is
not kept up to date, so it is not a backup. **Clone URL** on the website
copies a public repository once. A private repository is backed up from the
desktop app, as below.

## 1. Copy the repository to your computer

Open a terminal and run (put in your friend's GitHub name and the repository
name from its github.com address):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY.git ~/Backups/REPOSITORY
```

For a private repository Git asks for a username and a password. Type your
GitHub username, and for the password paste a **GitHub access token**, not
your GitHub password (GitHub no longer accepts passwords here). To make one,
on github.com open **Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens**:

- If the repository belongs to you or to an organization you are in, choose a
  **fine-grained token**, limit it to that one repository, and set
  **Contents** to **Read-only**. It cannot change anything.
- If the repository belongs to a friend's personal account, GitHub does not
  let fine-grained tokens reach it; use a **classic token** with the `repo`
  scope and an expiry date. That token can also write, so keep it private.
  Git uses it only on your computer; ForkMesh never sees it.

## 2. Add it to ForkMesh as a private repository

1. In the desktop app open **Repos** and choose **Import folder…**.
2. Pick the folder you just cloned (`~/Backups/REPOSITORY`).
3. ForkMesh asks **Import REPOSITORY?**. Choose **Private**.

**Private** means the copy is encrypted before it leaves your computer, is
hidden from public browsing and cloning, and only you (and people you share it
with) can read it. Do not choose **Public**: that lists it for anyone.

## 3. Keep it up to date

While the desktop app is open, ForkMesh checks the folder about once a minute
and copies anything new to the ForkMesh network (change how often under
**Settings → Mirror sync**). ForkMesh does not fetch from GitHub by itself yet, so bring in your
friend's newest changes by pulling them into the folder:

```sh
git -C ~/Backups/REPOSITORY pull
```

ForkMesh then copies them within the next sync. Pull as often as you want a
fresh backup, for example once a week.

## 4. Check the backup

Open the repository in **Repos** and look at its settings: it shows
**Managed mirror enabled** and **Last sync** with a time. A recent time means
the ForkMesh copy matches the folder on your computer.

## Things that will not happen

- Nothing is changed on GitHub or on your live website: clone and pull only
  read. Avoid the **Push** button and `git push` until you mean to change the
  website.
- Nothing becomes public unless you choose **Public**.
- Removing the repository from ForkMesh does not delete it from GitHub.

Back to [Getting started](getting-started.md) or the
[documentation index](README.md).

pages.title: Voice and video calls
pages.description: You can call anyone you have a direct message with, or everyone in a private channel at once. Calls work on the web at /chat, on iPhone and on Android. The desktop app has no…
pages.markdown:
# Voice and video calls

You can call anyone you have a direct message with, or everyone in a private
channel at once. Calls work on the web at `/chat`, on iPhone and on Android.
The desktop app has no call engine of its own: its call buttons open the call
in your browser and ask before anything rings.

## Start a call

1. Open the direct message and press the phone button (voice) or the camera
   button (video) in the header.
2. A pre-call check opens first. You see your camera, can pick a face,
   background or voice filter, and can press **Record a 10-second test clip**
   to hear exactly what the other person will get.
3. Press **Start voice call** or **Start video call**. Only now does it ring.

The other person's phone rings on any screen. An iPhone shows the system call
screen, even when it is locked or ForkMesh is closed, and even with
notifications turned off. The push notification never names the caller; the
app shows the name once it has opened the encrypted invite. A call nobody
answers leaves a "Missed audio call" or "Missed video call" line in the
conversation. A declined call leaves nothing, and the caller sees "Call
declined" or "Busy" with the reason.

## During a call

- **Back to chat** shrinks the call into a small window with Mute, Hang up
  and Open. Drag it anywhere; tap it or press Open to make it large again.
  The web remembers where you left it.
- Until the other person's video arrives, or while their camera is off, you
  see your own camera and their name instead of a black screen.
- On iPhone, video calls play through the loudspeaker, like FaceTime. Voice
  calls use the earpiece. The ring/silent switch does not mute a call.
- On iPhone, app sounds, speech and dictation leave your microphone alone
  while a call runs. During someone else's call (a phone call, Signal,
  FaceTime) ForkMesh stays quiet too.

## When the connection drops

A call reconnects by itself after a network drop, or when the other person's
audio goes silent while the connection still looks fine. The call says
"Reconnecting…" meanwhile. If it is not back within 30 seconds it ends with
"Call lost". A call that never connects ends after 30 seconds with "Could not
connect". If your microphone is unplugged or interrupted, the call opens it
again and says "Microphone reconnected".

One-to-one media goes straight between the two devices, with no relay server
in between. Two people who are both behind strict networks (some mobile
carriers and office firewalls) may not be able to connect at all.

## Call quality and Diagnose

Every call shows a small pill with four signal bars, a voice waveform (you up,
the other side down) and the round trip time. Four bars is a good connection,
one a poor one. Click the pill to open charts of your voice, the network and,
on video calls, the video in and out.

Next to it, **Diagnose** is grey while it measures, green while the call is
fine, and red when
it finds a lasting problem: high latency, lost packets, jitter, video held
back by bandwidth or by your device, a low frame rate, or a slow face filter.
Press it to see each problem, why it matters and the fixes in order. **Copy
prompt** gives you a ready question for an AI assistant; paste its `LESSON:`
line back and the next prompt starts from it. Fixes that worked on your
device move up the list. Nothing is sent anywhere: the report stays on your
device.

Voice is sent at up to 128 kbps with protection against lost packets, and when
the network is tight the call keeps your voice and lowers the picture first.

## Group calls

In a private channel, the same buttons start a group call for up to 16 people.
Members who are not in it see "A call is in progress here" with a Join button.
Public channels have no group calls, because their messages are readable by
the server. On the web, stay on the channel during the call: if you switch to
another one, people who join meanwhile see a blank tile for you until you
come back.

## Verification codes

Group calls on ForkMesh's newer call engine (on iPhone, and on the web in
browsers that support it) show four emoji with their names and "Or compare
numbers: 123 456". Read them aloud with everyone and press **They match** or
**They don't match**. The code changes when someone joins, and the panel says
who is not verified yet. If the codes differ, someone may be listening in:
leave the call and tell the others another way. A tile warns you when a
person's video cannot be confirmed as theirs or fails a check. Scanning a QR
code instead, and remembering verified people between calls, are not built
yet.

## What is encrypted

- **One-to-one calls.** The messages that set up the call are sealed with
  chat encryption, so the relay sees only ciphertext and stores none of it.
  Audio and video are encrypted and go directly between the two devices. The
  relay learns that a call is ringing in a conversation and when, not whether
  it is voice or video.
- **Group calls.** Each sender encrypts every audio and video frame on their
  device. ForkMesh's call server forwards the frames without being able to
  decrypt them. On the newer engine the keys use post-quantum key exchange and
  each sender signs their media, so nobody in the call can fake someone
  else's picture.
- Face, background and voice filters run on your device.

See [Chat encryption and integrations](security/sealed-chat.md) for how chat
itself is sealed, and [Safety numbers and trusted devices](chat-safety-numbers.md)
for checking who you are talking to.

## On Android

Android has one-to-one calls with the pre-call check and the quality pill.
Group calls, automatic reconnecting, the small call window, the Diagnose
button and the loudspeaker change arrive on iPhone first and are still being
ported. See [ForkMesh apps](apps.md).

pages.title: Safety numbers and trusted devices
pages.description: Direct messages are end-to-end encrypted to each device of the two people in the conversation. Every browser, phone and desktop you sign in on has its own chat key. A safety…
pages.markdown:
# Safety numbers and trusted devices

Direct messages are end-to-end encrypted to each device of the two people in
the conversation. Every browser, phone and desktop you sign in on has its own
chat key. A safety number lets you check that nobody else's key has slipped
into the conversation, and new devices wait for your approval before they get
anything.

Approvals and safety numbers are for direct messages. Channels accept every
correctly signed device on their own; see
[Chat encryption and integrations](security/sealed-chat.md).

## What a safety number is

A safety number is 60 digits in 12 groups of five, plus a QR code. You and the
other person see the same number, and it covers every approved device on both
sides. To find it:

- **Web.** Press the lock button ("End-to-end") in the conversation header.
  The Chat encryption panel shows the number under **Safety number**.
- **iPhone.** Open the conversation's details and tap **Safety number**. It
  shows the digits, your QR code and **Scan their code**.
- **Android.** Open **Safety number** from the conversation's menu.

Compare the digits in person or over a call you trust, or scan the other
phone's code. Then press **Mark as verified**. A scan tells you whether it
matched, or whether you scanned the wrong code.

## When it changes

The number changes whenever the set of approved devices changes: someone
approves a new phone or browser, or a device gets a new key. The change clears
"verified", and the conversation says "Your safety number with Alex changed".
If nobody you know added a device, compare the number again before you share
anything sensitive: a key nobody expected can mean someone is trying to read
along.

## New devices wait for you

In a direct message, the first device you see for a person is trusted. Every
further device for that person, including a new device of your own, waits.
It gets nothing sealed to it and its messages are held, unseen, until you
decide. The conversation shows "A new device for Alex wants to join this chat.
Check the safety number, then approve or block." and a banner with
**Safety number**, **Approve** and **Block**.

- **Approve** lets it receive new messages and opens the ones it sent while it
  waited (the most recent ones, if it sent many).
- **Block** keeps it out.
- A new device reads only messages sealed after it was approved, never the
  older history.

When several devices are waiting at once, for example after someone signs in
on a new phone and a new browser, the iPhone shows one banner for all of them
("2 new devices for Alex want to join this chat"), and Approve and Block act
on all of them. The web shows one device at a time and says how many are
waiting. On Android the single banner is still being ported.

## Reinstalling on iPhone

Your iPhone keeps a projects folder, by default in iCloud Drive, that survives
deleting the app. It holds your identity key, encrypted with your passphrase.
When you reinstall ForkMesh and press **Restore**, the app rebuilds your chat
key from that identity key. Your safety numbers stay the same, the people you
chat with see no new device, and a conversation you had verified stays
verified.

- This works only when the folder outlives the app. If the folder sits inside
  the app (On My iPhone › ForkMesh), it is deleted with the app, and ForkMesh
  warns you at every launch with "Keep your ForkMesh data safe" until you move
  it.
- If your iPhone set up chat before this was added (October 2026), it keeps
  its older chat key until the next reinstall. That one reinstall changes your
  safety numbers once; after it they survive.
- Restoring the key does not unlock old messages: the keys that opened them
  are not part of it.
- On Android, keeping the chat key through a reinstall is still being
  ported.

Related: [Voice and video calls](calls.md) has verification codes for group
calls, and [Portable identities and recovery](portable-identities.md) covers
your identity key.

pages.markdown:
# Mirror and deploy a Cloudflare Worker with ForkMesh

You already have a Cloudflare Worker and a GitHub repository for it. This guide
makes ForkMesh a signed mirror of that repository and the place your Worker is
deployed from. Each push to the default branch deploys automatically. You can
also deploy, watch the log, approve and roll back from your phone.

Your Cloudflare token stays on your own ForkMesh desktop. It never goes to
GitHub, the ForkMesh relay or a shared runner.

## How it fits together

```text
GitHub push ──► GitHub Actions bridge ──► ForkMesh (ssh.forkmesh.com)
                                              │
                                              ▼
                     your ForkMesh desktop  (label: cloudflare-deploy)
                     .forkmesh/deploy-cloudflare.yml
                                              │  wrangler deploy
                                              ▼
                                     Cloudflare Workers

ForkMesh phone app ──► desktop (LAN or relay): Run · Re-run · Approve · Roll back
```

| Piece | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `.github/workflows/forkmesh-github-sync.yml` | Copies branches and tags between GitHub and ForkMesh on every push and every 15 minutes, fast-forward only ([Connecting to GitHub](github-sync.md)) |
| `.forkmesh/deploy-cloudflare.yml` | Runs on your desktop when the default branch moves, or when you start it by hand |
| `.forkmesh/rollback-cloudflare.yml` | Started by hand: rolls the Worker back to its previous version |
| `.forkmesh/cloudflare-deploy.py` | Checks the setup, runs Wrangler and reports the deployed URL and version |
| `.forkmesh/cloudflare-deploy.json` | Worker folder, Wrangler environment, branch and variable names |

## Before you start

On the computer that will deploy (your ForkMesh desktop):

- the ForkMesh desktop, signed in to your account. Desktop Actions run on
  **Linux** only. They need `bwrap` (bubblewrap), a systemd user session, and
  a desktop that is not running as root.
- **Node.js 22 or newer** and **npm**, installed system-wide; current Wrangler
  needs Node.js 22. Many distributions still ship an older `nodejs`, so
  check `node --version`; [NodeSource](https://github.com/nodesource/distributions)
  packages install into `/usr`. Runs see `/usr` but not your home folder, so a
  Node.js installed with `nvm` is not found.
- `python3` and `git`.

You also need:

- a **Cloudflare API token**. In the Cloudflare dashboard, open *My Profile →
  API Tokens → Create Token* and use the **Edit Cloudflare Workers** template.
  Limit it to the account and zones the Worker uses.
- your **Cloudflare account ID**: 32 hexadecimal characters, shown in the
  dashboard's Workers overview.
- admin rights on the GitHub repository, and the `gh` command-line tool
  (optional, but it makes setting secrets easier).
- a ForkMesh repository with the same name. Create an empty one under
  **Repositories → New** on [app.forkmesh.com](https://app.forkmesh.com).
- the ForkMesh tools:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://forkmesh.com/forkmesh/forkmesh ~/forkmesh-tools
```

## Step 1: connect the repository

Run `connect` in a checkout of your Worker's GitHub repository. It writes the
deploy files above and the GitHub sync files, and adds `github` and `forkmesh`
remotes:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/NAME && cd NAME
python3 ~/forkmesh-tools/tools/cloudflare_worker_deploy.py connect \
  --github OWNER/NAME \
  --bridge-key-out ~/forkmesh-bridge.pem
```

Add these options as needed:

| Option | Use it when |
| --- | --- |
| `--worker-dir worker` | `wrangler.toml` / `wrangler.json(c)` is not at the repository root |
| `--env production` | you deploy a Wrangler environment (`[env.production]`) |
| `--branch release` | you deploy from a branch other than `main` |
| `--manual-only` | you only want deploys you start yourself, never on push |
| `--needs .forkmesh/ci.yml` | a ForkMesh test workflow must pass first |
| `--forkmesh OWNER/NAME` | the ForkMesh repository has a different owner or name |
| `--runs-on LABEL` | you want a desktop label other than `cloudflare-deploy` |
| `--token-variable NAME`, `--account-variable NAME` | different Workers deploy to different Cloudflare accounts |
| `--replace-vars` | Wrangler may delete dashboard variables that are missing from your config (by default they are kept, with `--keep-vars`) |
| `--no-rollback` | you do not want the roll-back workflow |

`connect` prints a JSON summary. Its `nextSteps` list is a checklist of the
remaining steps, and `existingGitHubDeploys` lists GitHub workflows that
already deploy this Worker. Running `connect` again is safe: it only rewrites
files whose content changed.

## Step 2: let GitHub push to ForkMesh

The bridge workflow pushes to ForkMesh over SSH. Give it its own key:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C forkmesh-sync -f ~/forkmesh-sync
```

1. Add `~/forkmesh-sync.pub` to your ForkMesh account under
   **Settings → SSH keys** (`/dashboard/settings/ssh-keys`). The key acts with
   your account's write access.
2. Store the secrets in GitHub:

```bash
gh secret set FORKMESH_BRIDGE_SIGNING_KEY --repo OWNER/NAME < ~/forkmesh-bridge.pem
gh secret set FORKMESH_SYNC_SSH_KEY --repo OWNER/NAME < ~/forkmesh-sync
gh variable set FORKMESH_SYNC_REMOTE --repo OWNER/NAME \
  --body ssh://git@ssh.forkmesh.com/OWNER/NAME.git
```

To pin the server's identity, also set the `FORKMESH_SYNC_KNOWN_HOSTS`
variable to this line:

```text
@cert-authority ssh.forkmesh.com,*.forkmesh.com ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAII5OvM7x8w4o1auHqYiSObIWHaVdAy4tT8dxLOai76Vs
```

## Step 3: prepare your desktop

1. **Add the repository.** In the desktop, open **Repositories** and clone
   `OWNER/NAME` from ForkMesh. The desktop now holds a mirror of the
   repository and receives each commit the bridge pushes.
2. **Label the desktop.** Under **Settings → Profile → Node labels**, add
   `cloudflare-deploy`. Only a node with this label runs the deploy. Mirrors
   and shared runners hold no secrets and skip it.
3. **Add the secrets.** Under **Settings → Secrets**, add:

| Name | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` | the API token from *Before you start* |
| `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` | your 32-character account ID |
| `FORKMESH_ACTIONS_ALLOW_NETWORK` | `1` |

   A run receives only the variables its workflow names, and their values are
   masked in logs. `FORKMESH_ACTIONS_ALLOW_NETWORK` gives every Actions run on
   this desktop network access, because Wrangler needs to reach Cloudflare.
4. **Turn on Actions for the repository.** In the repository's **Actions** tab,
   tick **Run actions on push**. Then read [Keep the token safe](#keep-the-token-safe)
   before you decide on **Automatically approve runs**.

## Step 4: turn off the old deploy

If GitHub or Cloudflare also deploys this Worker, each push deploys twice and
the last deploy wins. Before your first ForkMesh deploy:

- disable or delete the GitHub workflows listed in `existingGitHubDeploys`
  (`cloudflare/wrangler-action` or `wrangler deploy` steps);
- if the Worker uses **Workers Builds** (Cloudflare's own Git integration),
  disconnect the repository under *Worker → Settings → Build* in the Cloudflare
  dashboard.

Keep your GitHub test workflows: they still run on GitHub.

## Step 5: commit and deploy

```bash
git add .forkmesh .github/workflows/forkmesh-github-sync.yml
git commit -m "Mirror to ForkMesh and deploy the Worker from it"
git push origin HEAD
```

The bridge copies the commit to ForkMesh within a minute or two, and your
desktop starts **Deploy Cloudflare Worker**. If you turned off
**Automatically approve runs**, the run waits until you approve it in the
desktop's Actions tab or from your phone. A successful run ends with a line
like:

```text
::cloudflare-deploy:: ok worker=shop version=1b2c3d4e-… url=https://shop.example.workers.dev
```

The first step, `check --online`, stops the run before anything is deployed if
the token, account ID, Node.js or network is wrong. See
[Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

## Deploy from your phone

Install the ForkMesh app for iPhone or Android and sign in to the same account
as your desktop. The app finds your desktop by itself, with no pairing code:
on the same Wi-Fi it connects directly, and away from home it goes through the
end-to-end encrypted relay. Open the app once on the same network as your
desktop; if the connection away from home is refused, open it on that network
again. See [Mobile access](mobile/mobile-agent-access.md).

Open the repository, then **Actions**:

| You want to | In the app |
| --- | --- |
| Deploy now | **Deploy Cloudflare Worker → Run**, branch `main` |
| Undo a bad deploy | **Roll back Cloudflare Worker → Run** |
| Let a held run start | open the run, **Approve** (or **Reject**) |
| Retry a failed deploy | open the run, **Re-run** |
| Stop a deploy | open the run, **Stop** |
| See what happened | open the run: steps and live log, ending with the URL and version |

Things to know:

- Your desktop must be switched on, signed in and online. A re-run you ask
  for while it is offline is queued and starts when the desktop reconnects.
- You can also ship from GitHub's mobile app: merge a pull request into the
  default branch, and the bridge and your desktop deploy it.
- The website on a phone lists the workflows and the runs that mirrors report.
  It cannot start or approve a run on your desktop; use the app for that.
- This guide is in the app too, under **Docs**.

## Keep the token safe

Anyone who can change `.forkmesh/` workflows on the default branch can make a
run read `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`. With the bridge, that includes everyone with
write access on GitHub. The desktop approves a workflow's exact content, so:

- untick **Automatically approve runs** for this repository if other people can
  push to it. Every changed workflow then waits until you approve it, which you
  can do from your phone;
- give the token only the **Edit Cloudflare Workers** permissions, for the one
  account and zone it needs;
- revoke and replace the token in Cloudflare if a run you did not expect ever
  reads it, then update **Settings → Secrets**.

Pull requests never run this workflow: it has no `pull_request` trigger, and the
bridge fetches pull request code only as data and never runs it.

## Several Workers or environments

- **Staging and production:** connect with `--env production` and keep the
  default deploy for `main`. To deploy staging from another branch, use a
  second checkout or repository; one repository holds one deploy
  configuration.
- **Monorepo:** use `--worker-dir` for the Worker you deploy from this
  repository.
- **Two Cloudflare accounts:** save the tokens under different names
  (`SHOP_CF_TOKEN`, `SHOP_CF_ACCOUNT`) and pass `--token-variable` and
  `--account-variable`.

## Moving off GitHub

To drop GitHub completely, import the repository (**Repositories → New →
GitHub**, see [Repository imports](repository-imports.md)) or push your
history to an empty ForkMesh repository. Then run `connect` without
`--github`. Pushes to ForkMesh's default branch deploy the same way.

## Troubleshooting

| The log says | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `bubblewrap (bwrap) is required` / `no configured ForkMesh Actions sandbox` | Run the deploy on a Linux desktop with `bubblewrap` installed |
| `Node.js is not installed on this node` / `Node.js 20 is too old` | Install system-wide Node.js 22+ (for example from NodeSource); a Node.js from `nvm` is not visible to runs |
| `… GiB of virtual address space` | Update the ForkMesh desktop; Wrangler reserves a large sparse address range |
| `Cloudflare's API is unreachable` | Add `FORKMESH_ACTIONS_ALLOW_NETWORK` = `1` under **Settings → Secrets** |
| `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN is empty` / `not a 32-character account ID` | Add or correct the secret under **Settings → Secrets** (names are case-sensitive) |
| `Cloudflare rejected the API token` | Create a new token from the **Edit Cloudflare Workers** template |
| `pins account_id … different account` | Your `wrangler.toml` names another account: fix `account_id` or the secret |
| `no wrangler.jsonc, wrangler.json, wrangler.toml` | Run `connect` again with `--worker-dir` |
| `skipped refs/heads/… is not refs/heads/main` | Expected: only the configured branch deploys |
| The run never starts | Check the `cloudflare-deploy` node label, **Run actions on push**, and whether the run is waiting for approval |
| GitHub commits never reach ForkMesh | Open the **ForkMesh GitHub sync** run on GitHub; check `FORKMESH_SYNC_REMOTE`, the SSH key, and that the ForkMesh repository exists |
| Two deploys per push | Turn off the GitHub or Workers Builds deploy (Step 4) |

## Command reference

`cloudflare_worker_deploy.py` is also copied into your repository as
`.forkmesh/cloudflare-deploy.py`:

```bash
python3 .forkmesh/cloudflare-deploy.py check            # config, Wrangler file, Node.js
python3 .forkmesh/cloudflare-deploy.py check --online   # plus token, account and Worker
python3 .forkmesh/cloudflare-deploy.py deploy --dry-run # build without uploading
python3 .forkmesh/cloudflare-deploy.py deploy
python3 .forkmesh/cloudflare-deploy.py rollback [--version VERSION_ID]
python3 .forkmesh/cloudflare-deploy.py render-workflow
```

`deploy` and `rollback` read `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`
from the environment, so you can also run them by hand from a terminal. Exit
codes: `0` success or skipped, `1` the deploy failed, `2` setup error, `75`
Cloudflare unreachable. Wrangler output is masked so the token never appears.

pages.markdown:
# Working with coding agents

ForkMesh publishes one guide written for coding agents such as Claude Code:
[app.forkmesh.com/forkmesh-agent.md](https://app.forkmesh.com/forkmesh-agent.md).
Hand it to your agent and it can start your own ForkMesh instance for you,
work on ForkMesh repositories, and open pull requests the way the ForkMesh
team does.

## What the guide covers

- **Starting an instance.** What your server needs, writing the settings
  file for the [start page](https://forkmesh.com/start), or running
  `install-instance.sh` over SSH yourself, and what to do once it is up.
- **Working on a repository.** Cloning, branching, pushing to a hosted
  repository, and small commits with one scope each.
- **Opening pull requests.** From the desktop app, the MCP server's
  `open_pr_from_branch`, or the signed HTTP API, and the rules that keep a
  pull request easy to accept: small, independent of the others, built on
  the current `main`, and confirmed on the server before it is called live.
- **Ground rules.** Ask before anything hard to undo, never print secrets,
  never delete ForkMesh data folders.

## Use it in one message

Copy this into Claude Code (the start page has a Copy button for it):

```text
Read https://app.forkmesh.com/forkmesh-agent.md and help me start my own ForkMesh instance. Ask me for anything you need first.
```

The agent asks for your server address, domain, admin account and repository
owner, writes the settings file, and tells you when to upload it on the start
page. Your SSH password or key and your admin password stay out of the file:
you type them into the page yourself, so the agent never sees them. It asks
before it runs anything on your server.

## Keep it in your repository without committing it

To have every session read the guide, save it next to your code and tell Git
to ignore it only in your clone:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://app.forkmesh.com/forkmesh-agent.md -o FORKMESH.md
echo FORKMESH.md >> .git/info/exclude
```

`.git/info/exclude` is a per-clone `.gitignore` that is never committed, so
the file stays yours. Add `FORKMESH.md` to `.gitignore` instead when the
whole team should ignore it. Then point your agent at it: add `@FORKMESH.md`
to an ignored `CLAUDE.md`, or start a session with "read FORKMESH.md".

Re-download it now and then; the guide changes as ForkMesh does.

## Connect the ForkMesh MCP server

The ForkMesh source ships an MCP server, `tools/forkmesh_mcp_server.py`,
and lists it in `.mcp.json`, so Claude Code opened in a ForkMesh checkout
finds it. Reading code, issues and notes needs no token. Writing (issues,
notes, pull requests) needs a device-local token from **Desktop → Settings →
MCP**. No MCP tool gives a shell, arbitrary file access, pushes or
administration.

## Related

- [Start your own instance](start-your-own-instance.md)
- [Start from a settings file](start-config.md)
- [Contributing](../../CONTRIBUTING.md), including the pull request workflow
- [Contribute with git only](contributing-with-git.md)

pages.markdown:
# Community-reviewed contextual placements

Approval means disclosed public evidence met an instance's current criteria
for a limited period; it is not an endorsement and can be appealed, suspended,
or expire. Criteria are served by `GET /api/world/community-ads/criteria`.
Proposals disclose sponsor, ownership, product, data use, tracking, labor,
accessibility, and impact evidence, with at least two public HTTPS sources.

Voting is one eligible verified account per proposal (active, email-verified,
at least seven days old), never wallet-weighted. Conflicted voters may only
abstain. Approval needs quorum and two-thirds of non-abstaining votes; review
deadlines are at most 180 days.

Each instance is disabled by default and chooses placement contexts and a
public revenue purpose. Placements receive only a coarse page context such as
`town-square` or `repository`; targeting does not use profiles, device or
country data, search terms, wallets, or behavioral history. Responses carry
`tracking: none`. Member text ads are a separate system,
[ForkMesh Ads](operations/ad-network.md); a community placement takes
priority.

Receipts use the `community_ad_revenue` ledger class. They are not user funds,
rewards, or on-chain transfers; the Worker does not custody money.

pages.markdown:
# Contribute with git only

You can contribute to a public repository on ForkMesh with plain `git` and a
browser. You do not need the desktop app. The steps match GitHub: fork, push a
branch to your fork, open a pull request.

The examples use `app.forkmesh.com`. On a self-hosted instance, use that
instance's address instead, for example `git.example.org`.

## 1. Fork the repository

Sign in with a verified email address, open the repository and click **Fork**
next to **Star** at the top of the page. ForkMesh creates `<you>/<repo>` in
your account. Your fork shares the original repository's history, so it is
ready at once, whatever the repository's size.

If you already have a fork, **Fork** opens it. The arrow next to **Fork** lists
everyone's forks.

## 2. Clone and add your fork as a remote

```bash
git clone https://app.forkmesh.com/<owner>/<repo>.git
cd <repo>
git remote add fork https://app.forkmesh.com/<you>/<repo>.git
```

`origin` stays the original repository, so `git pull` keeps you up to date.

## 3. Push a branch

```bash
git checkout -b my-change
git commit -am "Describe the change"
git push fork my-change
```

When git asks for a username and password, enter your ForkMesh account name or
email and your account password. A push credential from **Settings → SSH keys
→ Push code over HTTPS** also works as the password.

After the push, git prints the page to open:

```
remote: Open a pull request for 'my-change' by visiting:
remote:      https://app.forkmesh.com/<you>/<repo>/compare/main...my-change
```

## 4. Open the pull request

Open that link, write a title and a description, and click **Create pull
request**. The pull request goes to the original repository. Your browser signs
it, so the maintainer can check it came from your account. If the original is
a read-only mirror of a repository hosted elsewhere, the pull request is
opened on your fork instead, and the page says so.

A pull request opened from a branch of the same repository follows that
branch: push more commits (or force-push a rebase) and the pull request shows
them, with "pushed N commits" in its timeline. A pull request from a fork
records your branch as it was when you opened it. After you push more commits
to your fork, open the pull request and click **Update pull request**: it sends
your branch's current state as a new revision, and the comments and reviews
stay. Only the pull request's author can update it this way.

## Without a fork

Some repositories let contributors push straight to them. There, push a branch
named `pr/<your-account>/<topic>` to the original repository and open the pull
request from the link git prints. See
[Contributing without write access](hosted-repositories.md#contributing-without-write-access).

## Good to know

- You can fork any public repository, whether it is hosted on ForkMesh's
  servers or published from someone's own node (like `forkmesh/forkmesh`). If
  you have a linked managed mirror, a fork of a node-published repository is
  made on your mirror instead.
- You can force-push your own branches after a rebase, amend or squash, which
  updates an open pull request. Use `git push --force-with-lease`: it refuses
  when the branch has commits you have not fetched (say, after **Update
  branch** on the pull request). If that happens, run `git pull --rebase` and
  push again. The default branch and protected branches only move forward,
  and the previous tip of a force-pushed branch is kept, so reviews of older
  commits still resolve.
- A pull request sent from your own copy as a patch series has no branch
  here to force-push: send the new commits with **Update pull request** on
  its page, which signs a revision of the same pull request.
- A push never deletes a branch. Delete branches on the fork's **Branches**
  page.
- Forks have their own per-account limit, separate from the repositories you
  create.
- If git says `Authentication failed`, check the account name or email and the
  password. [Git errors](git-errors.md) lists every message ForkMesh sends.

pages.description: For a project that could disappear soon. A plan (forkmesh-crisis-preservation-plan-v1) orders the work to fit the time and access left; an assessment…
pages.markdown:
# Preservation-first crisis onboarding

For a project that could disappear soon. A plan
(`forkmesh-crisis-preservation-plan-v1`) orders the work to fit the time and
access left; an assessment (`forkmesh-crisis-preservation-assessment-v1`) and a
drill (`forkmesh-crisis-preservation-drill-v1`) report what is actually safe.
One pure reference implementation backs the API, CLI, and fixture.

## Start here

```sh
curl -s 'https://app.forkmesh.com/api/preservation/crisis-plan?scenario=urgent_takedown&minutes=45'
tools/forkmesh_crisis_preservation.py plan urgent_takedown --minutes 45
```

Work through `steps` in order: a [resumable import](repository-imports.md), a
pushed local clone, a [portable identity](portable-identities.md) export, or a
mirror request. Read `tradeoffs` first; an urgent plan that leaves anything out
sets `acknowledgementRequired`. Afterwards, assess the migration report and the
mirrors payload:

```sh
tools/forkmesh_crisis_preservation.py assess request.json \
  --report report.json --availability mirrors.json
```

## Scenarios

Request fields: `scenario`, optional `minutes` (1 to 525,600), `access`
(`owner`, `read`, `public`, `none`), `sizeMb`, `issues`, `releases`,
`assetsMb`, `private`, `localClone`. Missing sizes use defaults listed in
`assumed`.

### `planned_shutdown`

Known end date, account still controlled. Window 30 days, access `owner`.
Priority: `refs`, `releases`, `documentation`, `issues`, `artifacts`, `identity_proofs`, `trusted_mirrors`.
Drill budget: **120 minutes**.

### `urgent_takedown`

Removal could happen any moment; always urgent. Window 1 hour, access `owner`.
Priority: `refs`, `identity_proofs`, `trusted_mirrors`, `releases`, `documentation`, `issues`, `artifacts`.
Drill budget: **30 minutes**.

### `lost_account`

Provider account lost; access capped at `public`. Window 1 day. Private data is
only preservable from a `localClone`.
Priority: `refs`, `identity_proofs`, `trusted_mirrors`, `releases`, `documentation`, `issues`, `artifacts`.
Drill budget: **60 minutes**.

### `censorship`

Blocked in a region or by the provider. Window 4 hours, access `public`.
Independent operators in different regions matter most; see the
[availability proof](availability-proof.md).
Priority: `refs`, `trusted_mirrors`, `identity_proofs`, `releases`, `documentation`, `artifacts`, `issues`.
Drill budget: **60 minutes**.

### `provider_eol`

Provider or product discontinued. Window 7 days, access `owner`.
Priority: `refs`, `releases`, `documentation`, `issues`, `artifacts`, `identity_proofs`, `trusted_mirrors`.
Drill budget: **120 minutes**.

## How a plan is built

The plan walks the priority order and includes each category whose
conservative estimate fits the remaining time. The import copies issues,
releases, and documentation in a fixed phase order, so a deferred import
category defers every later one. A plan is urgent for `urgent_takedown` or a
window of 240 minutes or less. `refs` is always included, flagged when it
exceeds the window.

## Reasons

### `time_budget`

Higher-priority data uses the available time.

### `requires_token`

The source is private and the current access cannot read it.

### `source_unreachable`

The source is gone (`access: none`) and no local clone holds the data.

### `import_order`

An earlier import phase did not fit, so this one will not be reached.

### `needs_refs`

Mirrors can only be requested once `refs` is preserved.

### `over_budget`

`refs` is required but its estimate exceeds the window.

## Coverage states

Only evidence can make a category `preserved` or `empty`; without evidence the
plan decision maps to `missing`, `skipped`, or `unavailable`.

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `preserved` | Evidence proves a complete copy. |
| `empty` | Evidence proves the source has none. |
| `partial` | Evidence proves only some of it. |
| `failed` | The attempt produced nothing usable. |
| `missing` | Planned, no evidence yet. |
| `skipped` | Deferred by the plan. |
| `unavailable` | Out of reach with the access available. |

`refs` needs an availability proof with a verified copy carrying every branch;
a migration report alone is `partial`. `trusted_mirrors` needs a `quorum`
proof. Report rows are recomputed, not trusted. `status` is `preserved`,
`partial` (a verified usable mirror exists), or `at_risk`.

## Risks to understand

### `ownership`

A copy does not transfer ownership; keep license and attribution.

### `legal`

Each node operator answers legal requests for their own node. See the
[node operator policy](operations/node-operator-policy.md).

### `secrets`

A mirror copies every committed secret; rotate them first. See
[secret scanning](security/secret-scanning.md).

### `verification`

Only a reconciled, signed migration report and an availability proof count.

### `external_dependencies`

Artifact bytes, wikis, CI logs, and registries are not imported; the report
lists them under `externalDependencies`.

### `emergency_contacts`

Report compromised accounts or keys to **security@forkmesh.com**.

## Getting help without lock-in

| Route | Who | Payment | Available |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `self_serve` | You, with an import and your own mirror node | No | Yes |
| `community_mirror` | Independent operators via the Mirrors tab | No | Yes |
| `managed_recovery` | Paid verified recovery | Yes | No |

Every route exits through `git clone --mirror`, the signed report, and the
identity kit. See the [business model](business-model.md).

## Drills

A drill records `startedAt` and `verifiedAt` (ms) plus evidence, and passes
within its scenario's drill budget with no failures:

```sh
tools/forkmesh_crisis_preservation.py drill drill.json
```

| Failure | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `invalid_timing` | Timestamps missing or reversed. |
| `over_time_budget` | Took longer than the budget. |
| `no_migration_report` | No readable report. |
| `migration_report_unreconciled` | Report incomplete or rows do not add up. |
| `no_verified_mirror` | No verified copy carries every branch. |

## API and conformance

`GET /api/preservation/crisis-plan` returns the
`forkmesh-crisis-preservation-catalog-v1` catalog, or a plan when `scenario` is
given. It is public, cached five minutes, stores nothing, and returns `400` with
a closed code on bad input. Assessments and drills run locally only. CLI exit
codes: 0 success, 3 at risk or failed, 2 unreadable input. Migration metrics
are under [migration reports](repository-imports.md#migration-reports).

Model and fixture: `conformance/crisis-preservation/v1/` (`model.json`,
`fixture-input.json`, `generate_fixture.py --check`). Tests:
`app/tests/test_crisis_preservation.py`.

pages.description: Builds that depend on Git sources must install the same bytes when the hosting provider changes or the origin disappears. Contract: conformance/dependencies/v1/contract.json…
pages.markdown:
# Stable repository identity and dependency workflows

Builds that depend on Git sources must install the same bytes when the hosting
provider changes or the origin disappears. Contract:
`conformance/dependencies/v1/contract.json`; reference rules:
`app/src/stable_repository.py`; probe: `tools/dependency_conformance.py`.
Stock clients need no ForkMesh tooling.

## Identity and pinning

| Concept | Value | Changes when moved? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Logical identity | `urn:forkmesh:repository:sha256:<64 hex>` (FM-ID-001 over `git-root-commit:<root>` from the signed catalog record) | No |
| Pinned content | Full 40- or 64-hex commit ID | No |
| Routes | `https://HOST/OWNER/REPOSITORY[.git]`, `ssh://git@HOST/OWNER/REPOSITORY.git` | Yes |

Hosts, owners, aliases, names and URLs are routing hints only. A record with no
root commit has no identity (empty string). The
[repository index](repository-index.md) returns `identity` on every result.

A pin is identity plus full commit ID. The resolver rejects branches, tags and
short IDs (`mutable_pin`), malformed identities (`identity_invalid`) and refs
outside `refs/heads/` or `refs/tags/` (`ref_invalid`).

## Switching providers without editing a lock

Write manifests and locks against one logical base URL and point it at the
active provider:

```sh
git config --global url."https://ACTIVE-PROVIDER/".insteadOf "https://LOGICAL-HOST/"
```

All recipes run Git underneath, so locks stay byte-identical; rollback restores
the previous line. `LOGICAL_URL` is `https://LOGICAL-HOST/OWNER/REPOSITORY.git`.

### Git

`git clone LOGICAL_URL dep && git -C dep checkout --detach COMMIT` (evidence:
`git rev-parse HEAD`).

### Git submodule

`git submodule add LOGICAL_URL deps/dep`, then check out `COMMIT` (evidence: the
gitlink in the superproject tree).

### pip

`dependency @ git+LOGICAL_URL@COMMIT` (evidence: `vcs_info.commit_id` in
`direct_url.json`).

### npm

`"dependency": "git+LOGICAL_URL#COMMIT"` (evidence: `resolved` in
`package-lock.json`).

### Go modules

`GOPROXY=direct GOPRIVATE=LOGICAL-HOST go get LOGICAL-HOST/OWNER/REPOSITORY.git@COMMIT`
(evidence: `go.sum` hashes; a moved tag fails with a checksum mismatch).

### Cargo

`dependency = { git = "LOGICAL_URL", rev = "COMMIT" }` with
`CARGO_NET_GIT_FETCH_WITH_CLI=true` (evidence: `source` line in `Cargo.lock`).

## Fallback

The relay checks candidate hosts in declared order before sending any bytes. A
route is skipped as `unreachable`, `identity_mismatch`, `state_unverified`
(refs do not hash to a signed state), `commit_missing` or `ref_moved`.
Resolution status:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `resolved` | The first route proved the content. |
| `failed_over` | A later route proved it; skipped routes are listed with reasons. |
| `unavailable` | No route proved it; nothing is served. |
| `rejected` | The pin itself is unusable. |

There is never a silent fallback to unverified or mutable content.

## Scenarios

`tools/dependency_conformance.py run` builds loopback providers (origin, mirror,
tampered copy, retagged copy) and runs every client through:

| Scenario | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| `install` | Installs the pinned commit. |
| `provider-switch` | Installs via `insteadOf`; lock identical. |
| `origin-lost` | `failed_over` to the mirror; lock identical. |
| `unverified-fallback` | Refused with `state_unverified`. |
| `missing-commit` | Fails with `commit_missing`. |
| `moved-tag` | Fails with `ref_moved`. |
| `rollback-recovery` | `resolved` again; lock identical. |

The report (`forkmesh-dependency-conformance-report-v1`) summary carries
`resolutionSuccess`, `resolutionAttempts`, `failoverSuccess`,
`failoverAttempts`, `reproducibleLocks`, `lockChecks`, `verificationFailures`,
`unexpectedResults` (must be 0) and `unavailableClients`. Reports contain no
paths, loopback URLs, contents, credentials or addresses.

```sh
python3 tools/dependency_conformance.py validate
python3 tools/dependency_conformance.py run --output report.json [--clients git,pip --require git,pip]
```

`run` exits 0 on success, 1 on an unexpected result or missing required client,
2 when it cannot run. It only reads: pushes (over SSH, or over HTTPS with an
account credential) are out of scope, and only public repositories and direct
Git installs are covered.

pages.description: This guide prepares a community for losing its normal infrastructure: the origin host is wiped, the hosted service is down, names stop resolving, a signing key is lost, a region…
pages.markdown:
# Disaster recovery

This guide prepares a community for losing its normal infrastructure: the
origin host is wiped, the hosted service is down, names stop resolving, a
signing key is lost, a region is cut off, or a backup is corrupt. It covers
preparation, recovery, and proving recovery works.

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [runbook.md](runbook.md) | The printable runbook: triage, roles and checklists, prerequisites, a decision tree per scenario, procedures with verification and rollback, and an exercise worksheet. |
| [exercise-register.md](exercise-register.md) | Every recorded exercise, its findings and corrective owners, and what closure still needs. |
| [`conformance/disaster-recovery/v1/runbook.json`](../../../conformance/disaster-recovery/v1/runbook.json) | The runbook source (`forkmesh-disaster-runbook-v1`). `runbook.md` is generated from it. |
| `tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py` | Validates and renders the runbook, builds and verifies the bootstrap kit, manages the roster and key rotations, and runs drills. |

The runbook builds on
[offline and low-bandwidth sync](../offline-sync.md),
[transports and anonymity postures](../transports.md),
[self-hostable service roles](../operations/service-roles.md),
[node backup and recovery](../operations/node-backup-and-recovery.md), and
[portable identities](../portable-identities.md).

## Start here: prepare before a disaster

1. **Make keys.** One kit key, one export key per mirror operator, and one
   recovery key for each custodian. Keep the seeds on separate devices, held by
   different people.

   ```sh
   tools/forkmesh_offline_sync.py keygen kit.key          # prints the kit public key
   tools/forkmesh_offline_sync.py keygen export.key
   tools/forkmesh_offline_sync.py keygen recovery-1.key   # one per custodian
   ```

2. **Write the community roster** (below), then check it:

   ```sh
   python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py roster check roster.json
   ```

3. **Build the bootstrap kit** onto removable media, and write the kit public
   key and the manifest digest it prints on paper:

   ```sh
   python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py kit build /media/usb/forkmesh-kit \
     --signing-key kit.key --roster roster.json
   ```

4. **Print [runbook.md](runbook.md)** with its digest and the kit public key.
5. **Run the drills**, then tabletop and live exercises; record each one.

## The community roster

The roster (`forkmesh-recovery-roster-v1`) is how members find each other
without the website. It lists pinned keys, mirrors, and contacts, and it
travels inside the signed kit.

```json
{
  "schema": "forkmesh-recovery-roster-v1",
  "community": "example community",
  "updated": "2026-09-14",
  "recoveryThreshold": 2,
  "keys": [
    {"keyId": "export-1", "publicKey": "<base64url>", "role": "export", "holder": "Mirror operator A", "status": "active"},
    {"keyId": "recovery-1", "publicKey": "<base64url>", "role": "recovery", "holder": "Custodian 1", "status": "active"},
    {"keyId": "recovery-2", "publicKey": "<base64url>", "role": "recovery", "holder": "Custodian 2", "status": "active"},
    {"keyId": "recovery-3", "publicKey": "<base64url>", "role": "recovery", "holder": "Custodian 3", "status": "active"}
  ],
  "mirrors": [
    {"name": "library mirror", "urls": ["http://mirror.example.lan:8080/project.git", "http://10.0.0.20:8080/project.git"],
     "pinnedHosts": {"mirror.example.lan": "10.0.0.20"}}
  ],
  "contacts": [{"role": "coordinator", "name": "<name>", "channel": "<phone or radio>"}],
  "rotations": []
}
```

Key roles are `export` (signs removable media), `kit` (signs bootstrap kits),
and `recovery` (signs key rotations); status is `active` or `revoked`.
`roster check` exits 3 when the roster is invalid, has no active export key, or
has fewer distinct recovery holders than `recoveryThreshold`. It warns when no
mirror URL works without DNS (literal address, onion address, or a
`pinnedHosts` name), when one custodian can rotate keys alone, or when an export
key holder also holds a recovery key.

```sh
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py roster check roster.json [--json]
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py roster keys roster.json --role export
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py roster profile roster.json --out lan.json
```

`roster profile` writes a `lan-only` [transport profile](../transports.md#postures)
that dials the roster's pinned local addresses, so a clone needs no DNS.

## The bootstrap kit

A kit is a directory holding exactly what a community needs to recover with no
network: the runbook source and printable copy, the recovery tools, the guides
they cite, and the roster. Its manifest, `forkmesh-recovery-kit.json`, is a
`forkmesh-recovery-kit-signed-v1` envelope over a `forkmesh-recovery-kit-v1`
manifest listing every file's SHA-256 and size, the runbook version and digest,
the build date, and `reviewBy`.

```sh
python3 -B tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py kit verify /media/usb/forkmesh-kit \
  --trusted-key <kit key from paper>
```

Run it from the kit on the disconnected machine; it never opens a network
connection. It checks the signature against the key you pass (read it from
paper, never from the kit), that every listed file matches with no extras or
symlinks, that the runbook validates against the kit's own tools and guides and
matches its digest and printable copy, and that the roster verifies.

A key that starts with `-` must be joined to its flag:
`--trusted-key=-Ab…`. Written as two words, the tool reads the key as an
unknown option and exits with code 2.

| State | Exit code | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `verified` | `0` | Everything checked, and the kit is before its review date. |
| `stale` | `4` | Everything checked, but the kit is past `reviewBy`. Use it, then rebuild it from a current roster. |
| `failed` | `3` | Do not run anything from this kit. |

`--today YYYY-MM-DD` checks freshness as of another date.

## Key recovery

A lost or stolen export or kit key is replaced by a rotation signed by a
threshold of recovery custodians; no single custodian or lost key can do it.

```sh
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py key rotate --roster roster.json \
  --recovery-key recovery-1.key --revoke <lost key> --successor <new key> \
  --holder "<holder>" --reason "<reason>" --issued <YYYY-MM-DD> --out rotation.json
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py key cosign rotation.json --recovery-key recovery-2.key --roster roster.json
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py key apply roster.json rotation.json --out roster-rotated.json
```

The statement is `forkmesh-recovery-key-rotation-v1`, wrapped in
`forkmesh-recovery-key-rotation-signed-v1`. `key apply` refuses a rotation with:

| Code | Refused because |
| --- | --- |
| `statement_digest` | `statementSha256` does not match the statement. |
| `community_mismatch` | The rotation names another community. |
| `already_applied` | The roster already lists this rotation. |
| `bad_signature` | A signature does not verify. |
| `signer_not_recovery_key` | A signer is not an active recovery key. The lost key cannot sign its own replacement. |
| `below_threshold` | Fewer distinct recovery signatures than `recoveryThreshold`. |
| `revoke_unknown` | A revoked key is not an active key in the roster. |
| `revoke_recovery_key` | Recovery keys change only by building a new kit with the custodians present. |
| `successor_known` | The successor key is already in the roster. |
| `successor_role` | The successor must be an export or kit key. |
| `statement_invalid` | The successor key or issued date is malformed. |

Media signed by the revoked key then fails import; re-export from a verified
copy with the successor key. Never lower the threshold during an incident.

Mirror node identity keys move with the node's sealed identity export
([moving or replacing an identity key](../operations/node-backup-and-recovery.md#moving-or-replacing-an-identity-key)).
Personal identities recover with the portable recovery kit
([recovery drills](../portable-identities.md#recovery-drills)).

## Drills

Each scenario has a live drill that builds a small community in scratch space
(origin, mirror, maintainer clone, signed export, roster), causes the disaster,
recovers with the runbook's tools, and measures the result.

```sh
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py drill run all --report drills.json --telemetry drills.jsonl
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py drill run origin-loss --fault no-local-clone
```

| Scenario | What the drill does | Fault injection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `origin-loss` | Deletes the origin, restores from mirror plus maintainer clone, refuses a stale overwrite. | `no-local-clone` |
| `main-service-loss` | Stops the hosted copy and serves a read-only static mirror a newcomer clones and verifies. | `no-surviving-mirror` |
| `dns-loss` | Clones over a `lan-only` route with roster-pinned addresses; strace flags any DNS query. | `no-pinned-address` |
| `key-loss` | Refuses invalid rotations, applies a 2-of-3 rotation, refuses media forged with the lost key. | `threshold-unreachable` |
| `regional-isolation` | Two diverged regions exchange signed media; every commit reaches both. | `unpinned-region-key` |
| `corrupted-backup` | Rejects a corrupt backup and restores the previous verified one, recording loss. | `all-copies-corrupt` |
| `offline-bootstrap` | Verifies a kit and imports offline with the network blocked; refuses a tampered kit. | `wrong-kit-key` |

A `forkmesh-disaster-drill-report-v1` report records `recoveryMs`,
`withinObjective`, `dataLoss`, `missingPrerequisites`, `unsafeSteps`, each step
and check, and `verdict`. A drill passes only when every check passes within
budget, data loss is allowed by policy, and no blocking prerequisite is missing.
`--telemetry FILE` appends one count-only `forkmesh-disaster-drill-telemetry-v1`
line per drill with no paths, keys, names, or addresses.

## Exercises and evidence

Record every exercise as
`conformance/disaster-recovery/v1/exercises/DRX-NNNN.json`
(`forkmesh-disaster-exercise-v1`): kind (`tabletop` or `live`), status, runbook
version and digest, whether only the offline runbook was used, participants
with roles and familiarity (`unfamiliar`, `familiar`, `automation`), and per
scenario the result, recovery time, data loss, missing prerequisites, and
unsafe steps. Each missing prerequisite or unsafe step taken names a finding
with a corrective owner (`person`, runbook `role`, or `issue`).

Retain automated drill reports as content-addressed evidence, then cite them:

```sh
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py attest drills.json   # prints evidence/<sha256>.json references
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py render
python3 tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py gate
```

A row citing `drillReport` must match the report it cites. Editing the runbook
without bumping its version fails validation for exercises on that version.

## Closure

`closure` lists the unmet checks and exits 1 until all are met; the
[register](exercise-register.md) shows the same status.

| Check | Met when |
| --- | --- |
| `automated-drills-current` | Every scenario has a passing drill report on the current runbook digest. |
| `platform-evidence` | Those reports cover Linux, macOS, and Windows. |
| `tabletop-drills-recorded` | Every scenario was run as a tabletop exercise with at least two people. |
| `live-drills-recorded` | People recovered every scenario in a live exercise. |
| `unfamiliar-team-restored` | Two or more people unfamiliar with ForkMesh restored a verified network using only the offline runbook. |
| `findings-owned` | Every open finding has a named person as its corrective owner. |

Automation cannot meet the people checks.

## Clean restoration

When normal infrastructure returns:

- compare its refs with the restored network before anything syncs, and push
  restored work to it as fast-forwards only;
- keep any diverged branches under review, never force-push over them;
- stop emergency static mirrors and delete temporary transport profiles;
- apply any key rotations to every roster copy, then rebuild and re-sign the
  kit, and write the new key and digest on paper;
- write the exercise or incident record, with a corrective owner for every
  finding.

## Commands

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py validate` | Check the runbook's roles, prerequisites, decision trees, commands, guide headings, and kit completeness against the repository. |
| `forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py render [--check]` | Write or check `runbook.md` and `exercise-register.md`. |
| `forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py gate` | Validate the runbook, every exercise, and rendered output. |
| `forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py closure` | Report the closure checks. |
| `forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py roster check`, `roster keys`, `roster profile` | Roster commands (above). |
| `forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py key rotate`, `key cosign`, `key apply` | Key rotation (above). |
| `forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py kit build`, `kit verify` | Bootstrap kit (above). |
| `forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py drill run` | Live drills (above). |
| `forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py attest` | Retain drill reports as evidence. |

| Exit code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Done. |
| `1` | Validation, a drill, the gate, or closure failed. |
| `2` | Usage error or unreadable input. |
| `3` | A kit, roster, or rotation did not verify. |
| `4` | The kit verified but is past its review date. |

## Supported platforms

The drills need Git 2.40+ and Python 3.9+. The `disaster-recovery-conformance`
quality gate runs the test suite, and CI runs the suite, gate, and every drill
on Linux, macOS, and Windows. DNS leak tracing in the `dns-loss` drill needs
strace and runs only on Linux.

## Limits

- Drills do not build the Go mirror node; node archive restores and identity
  imports are covered by `server/nodeops_test.go` instead.
- The `search` and `organization-service` roles are hosted-only, so
  main-service loss cannot restore them.
- Kits are signed by one kit key, not a threshold.

pages.markdown:
# Disaster recovery exercise register

<!-- Generated by tools/forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py render from conformance/disaster-recovery/v1/exercises. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every tabletop and live exercise of the [disaster recovery runbook](runbook.md) is
recorded here with its recovery time, data loss, missing prerequisites, unsafe
steps, and a corrective owner for each finding. The guide is [README.md](README.md).

Current runbook: version 1.0.0, digest `b93908faaa80a062ef68b76c01bb1d452bd93cc0b83b821c483e25f0212229ee`.

## Closure status

| Check | Status | Still missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every scenario has a passing automated drill on the current runbook (`automated-drills-current`) | met | nothing |
| Automated drills pass on Linux, macOS, and Windows (`platform-evidence`) | open | origin-loss on macos, origin-loss on windows, main-service-loss on macos, main-service-loss on windows, dns-loss on macos, dns-loss on windows, key-loss on macos, key-loss on windows and 6 more |
| Every scenario has a tabletop exercise with people (`tabletop-drills-recorded`) | open | origin-loss, main-service-loss, dns-loss, key-loss, regional-isolation, corrupted-backup, offline-bootstrap |
| Every scenario has a live exercise in which people recovered (`live-drills-recorded`) | open | origin-loss, main-service-loss, dns-loss, key-loss, regional-isolation, corrupted-backup, offline-bootstrap |
| A team unfamiliar with ForkMesh restored a verified repository network from the offline runbook alone (`unfamiliar-team-restored`) | open | no such live exercise is recorded |
| Every open finding has a named person as corrective owner (`findings-owned`) | open | DRX-0001 F1 (owner: issue #518), DRX-0001 F2 (owner: issue #502), DRX-0001 F3 (owner: issue #518) |

## Exercises

### DRX-0001: Automated live drills of runbook 1.0.0 on Linux

Kind: live. Status: completed. Date: 2026-09-14. Runbook 1.0.0. Offline runbook only: no.

Every scenario's drill ran once in scratch space with `drill run all` on Linux (Git 2.47, Python 3.13), with strace tracing the dns-loss clone. No people took part, so this record cannot meet the tabletop, live, or unfamiliar-team closure checks.

| Participant | Roles | Familiarity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| forkmesh_disaster_recovery.py drill runner | coordinator, key-custodian, mirror-operator, verifier, scribe | automation |

| Scenario | Result | Recovery time | Data loss | Missing prerequisites | Unsafe steps | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `origin-loss` | recovered | 1.2 s | none | none | 1 refused, 0 taken | `50ac6d4412cd98d7` (pass, linux) |
| `main-service-loss` | recovered | 1.6 s | none | none | 1 refused, 0 taken | `868ed1351d6f34f0` (pass, linux) |
| `dns-loss` | recovered | 1.6 s | none | none | 0 refused, 0 taken | `1eb175b2a7922689` (pass, linux) |
| `key-loss` | recovered | 6.4 s | none | none | 3 refused, 0 taken | `c47b9ca4cd3d5ddd` (pass, linux) |

| `corrupted-backup` | recovered | 3.6 s | 1 commit newer than the last verified backup; allowed by since-last-good-copy | none | 1 refused, 0 taken | `4f913921e60f7b46` (pass, linux) |
