pages.title: ActivityPub federation (fediverse interop)
pages.description: The relay joins the ActivityPub network (Mastodon-compatible) with followable actors on its own domain.
pages.markdown:
# ActivityPub federation (fediverse interop)

The relay joins the ActivityPub network (Mastodon-compatible) with followable
actors on its own domain.

| Actor | Handle | Actor URL | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| User profile | `@alice@forkmesh.com` | `/ap/users/alice` | `Person` |
| Repository | `@owner.repo@forkmesh.com` | `/ap/repos/owner/repo` | `Group` |
| Service actor | `@forkmesh.com@forkmesh.com` | `/ap/actor` | `Application` |

User names never contain a dot, so `owner.repo` splits on the first dot.
Handles are lowercase. Only active public accounts and published public
repositories federate.

## What federates

**Outbound.** Verified signed-inbox submissions (issue, pull request and
discussion opens, comments and reviews) are posted as `Create(Note)` by the
repository actor and, when the author is a local account, by the user actor.
Releases and merges are announced through the owner-signed
`POST /api/repo/{owner}/{repo}/ap-publish`. Inline `data:` images in a body
(up to 4) are re-served at `/ap/o/{uuid}/media/{n}` and attached as `Image`.

**Inbound.** `Follow` (auto-accepted), `Undo(Follow)`, `Create(Note)` replies
and mentions, and `Delete`. Remote replies are stored as federated comments
(`GET /api/repo/{owner}/{repo}/fedi-comments`) and kept outside the
Ed25519-signed event log, because they can never carry a ForkMesh author
signature.

**Mentions never create issues automatically.** A verified public Note that
mentions a repository actor becomes an encrypted review record. The owner can
edit and explicitly authorize it as an issue-inbox submission; the feed says
`created` only after the owner's node commits the issue. A backlink reply is
sent only with separate consent.

## Wire protocol

- RSA-2048 key per actor, published as `publicKeyPem` (`<actor>#main-key`);
  private keys encrypted at rest.
- draft-cavage HTTP signatures (`rsa-sha256`). Outbound signs
  `(request-target) host date digest content-type`. Inbound requires
  `(request-target)` and `digest`, checks the digest byte for byte, enforces a
  ±12 h date window and requires the `keyId` host to match the actor. Remote
  keys are cached for 24 h with one forced refresh on failure.
- Discovery: `/.well-known/webfinger`, `/.well-known/nodeinfo` →
  `/nodeinfo/2.1`, and content negotiation on `/@name` and `/@owner.repo`.

The protocol core (documents, signing strings, digests, sanitization) is
`app/src/activitypub.py`, tested by `tests/test_activitypub.py`.

## Delivery

Each publish writes one `ap_outbox` row per destination inbox (shared inbox
preferred). A few are delivered inline; a periodic drain retries the rest with
exponential backoff (5 minutes to 24 hours, 8 attempts; 404/410 drop at once).
Actor keys are created lazily on first lookup.

## Profiles

- Instance and user actors fall back to the instance avatar and banner; a
  repository actor never uses instance branding.
- Repository owners can upload a logo and banner through
  `POST /api/repo/{o}/{r}/about`; otherwise the committed
  `.forkmesh/banner.png` and `logo.png` are used. The About description is the
  actor bio.
- Every actor publishes `PropertyValue` links (canonical page and relay)
  verified by a reciprocal `rel="me"` link.
- A repository actor's `url` is its `/@owner.repo` profile page.
- Saving a profile broadcasts `Update(actor)` to followers.
- Owners can list and delete federated posts (`POST /api/repo/{o}/{r}/ap-posts`);
  a delete sends `Delete(Tombstone)` to followers.

## Administration

Signed admin routes `GET /api/accounts/admin-ap` and
`POST /api/accounts/admin-ap-update` read state and switch federation:
`enable`/`disable` (while disabled every ActivityPub endpoint returns 404) and
`block`/`unblock` a domain, which rejects its activities and purges its
followers, cached actors and queued deliveries, subdomains included.
`PUBLIC_BASE_URL` sets the actor origin for self-hosted relays.

## Limitations

- Local users cannot follow remote accounts; inbound `Like`, `Announce` and
  `Update` are acknowledged and dropped.
- Follower collections expose `totalItems` only.

pages.title: Conflict-safe signed collaboration objects
pages.description: Status: normative protocol version 1, part of the ForkMesh protocol suite. Suite version: 1.0.0-rc.1. The machine-readable envelope schema is collaboration-event-v1.schema.json.…
pages.markdown:
# Conflict-safe signed collaboration objects

Status: normative protocol version 1, part of the
[ForkMesh protocol suite](../protocol/README.md). Suite version: `1.0.0-rc.1`. The machine-readable envelope schema is
[`collaboration-event-v1.schema.json`](../../public/docs/protocol/collaboration-event-v1.schema.json).
The dependency-free reference fold is `app/src/collaboration.py`; the independent
WebCrypto fold is `app/public/collaboration.js`.

## Invariants

ForkMesh collaboration state is a deterministic projection of an immutable set
of signed events. A relay, mirror, or database may transport and index those
events, but is never authoritative for their meaning. Given the same policy and
event set, implementations MUST produce the same state when events are
permuted, duplicated, delayed, or replayed.

Implementations MUST retain each canonical raw envelope. Materialized fields,
search indexes, counts, and notification views are disposable caches. Invalid
input is retained only in a bounded quarantine/audit channel and MUST NOT enter
the state fold.

## Repository, object, and event identity

A repository identity is:

```text
urn:forkmesh:repository:sha256:<sha256(
  "forkmesh-repository-identity-v1\n" || verified repository root
)>
```

The verified root is deployment-specific (for example a signed repository
manifest), but aliases and mutable URLs are not identities.

Every object's first event carries a random 16-byte `objectKey`, base64url
without padding. The object ID is:

```text
urn:forkmesh:collaboration:<family>:sha256:<sha256(
  "forkmesh-collaboration-object-v1\n" || canonical-json({
    repository, family, creator, objectKey, references
  })
)>
```

This binds the repository, family, creator, and immutable references before an
event is signed. For reactions, clients SHOULD derive `objectKey` from subject,
author, and normalized emoji to make one logical reaction idempotent. For
notifications, clients SHOULD derive it from recipient and causing event.

The event ID binds both the signed meaning and its deterministic Ed25519
signature:

```text
signingBytes = utf8("forkmesh-collaboration-event-v1\n") ||
               canonical-json(unsigned envelope)
eventId = "sha256:" || hex(sha256(signingBytes || 0x00 || rawSignature))
```

Ed25519 public keys are raw 32-byte keys and signatures are raw 64-byte values,
both base64url without padding. Schema/domain prefixes are frozen; changed
meaning requires a new version.

## Canonical encoding

The wire envelope is canonical JSON encoded as UTF-8 with no BOM or trailing
newline. Object keys are ASCII, sorted lexicographically; there is no
insignificant whitespace. Strings are NFC-normalized and lone surrogates are
forbidden. Values are objects, arrays, strings, booleans, null, or integers whose
magnitude is at most 2^53-1 (envelope counters are additionally
non-negative); floating point and duplicate object keys are forbidden. Arrays
whose semantics are sets (`parents`, `references`, observed IDs, and set
values) are sorted and duplicate-free. An envelope is at most 1 MiB and JSON
nesting is at most 32 levels, so malformed input cannot force unbounded parser
or canonicalizer work.

A receiver MUST parse with duplicate-key detection, reproduce the exact
canonical bytes, recompute `eventId`, and verify Ed25519 before considering
causality or authorization. Noncanonical encodings fail closed even if they
would parse to the same JSON value.

## Causality and replay defense

`parents` names the events observed when an author made an event. The Lamport
`clock` is zero without parents and otherwise exactly one plus the greatest
parent clock. `issuedAt` is display/audit time only and never decides a winner.

Each signing key allocates a repository-wide monotonically increasing
`sequence`. Gaps and concurrent slots from different keys are valid. Two
different events signed by one key in the same sequence slot are equivocation:
both are excluded and surfaced in audit telemetry. A sequence lower than or
equal to a same-author ancestor is a rollback and is rejected.

Missing-parent events remain pending, with their raw bytes retained. A child of
a rejected event is rejected; it cannot bypass validation by arriving first.
Duplicate event IDs are one logical event and only increment the replay metric.
Repository, object, policy, and schema binding prevents a valid signature from
being replayed into another context.

## References and policy

References are sorted `{relation, family, object}` triples. A comment has one
issue/PR/comment subject; a reaction has one issue/PR/comment/review subject; a
review has one PR subject; a moderation object has one non-notification,
non-moderation subject. References on every event for one object must exactly
match its first event, preventing later retargeting.

Every event binds the SHA-256 ID of a canonical repository policy document:

```json
{
  "schema": "forkmesh-collaboration-policy-v1",
  "repository": "urn:forkmesh:repository:sha256:…",
  "maintainers": ["<Ed25519 key>"],
  "moderators": ["<Ed25519 key>"],
  "notifiers": ["<Ed25519 key>"]
}
```

The repository trust root pins this document. Version 1 deliberately treats a
policy change as a new collaboration epoch; clients must retain the old epoch
and policy to verify history rather than re-authorizing old events under a new
role list.

| Family | Create | Later mutation / tombstone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Issue, pull request | Any signed identity | Creator or maintainer |
| Comment, reaction | Any signed identity | Creator; moderation is a separate decision |
| Review | Any signed identity | Creator; maintainer may dismiss via tombstone |
| Label, milestone, board | Maintainer | Maintainer |
| Notification | Recipient or policy notifier | Recipient |
| Moderation decision/resolution | Moderator | Moderator; subject creator may appeal |

Unauthorized events remain auditable but never influence state. Renderers MUST
NOT infer moderator power from an author name, server origin, arrival channel,
or possession of a database row.

Authority comes only from the policy document's keys. Implementations MUST NOT
infer any role from asset ownership or transaction history, and MUST NOT
require a wallet, token, blockchain account, payment, reward, tip, or bounty to
create, fold, authorize, moderate, or govern a collaboration object. Incentive
adapters may read folded state, but folded state never reads them; see
[incentive independence](../incentive-independence.md). Changing this rule is a
breaking protocol change.

## Fold and conflict rules

All families use the same primitives, with family-specific fields and role
rules:

| Family | Scalar registers | Observed-remove sets | Required reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Issue | title, body, status, priority, dueAt | labels, assignees | — |
| Pull request | title, body, status, base, head, mergeCommit | labels, reviewers | — |
| Comment | body | — | subject |
| Label | name, color, description | subjects | — |
| Reaction | emoji (immutable) | — | subject |
| Review | state, body, revision (immutable) | — | pull request |
| Milestone | title, description, status, dueAt | subjects | — |
| Board | name, description, status | items | — |
| Notification | kind/recipient (immutable), status, message | — | optional subject |
| Moderation | decision, reasonCode, note | — | subject |

For a scalar field, discard a candidate only when another write causally
descends it. One remaining value is current. Concurrent candidates with equal
values coalesce; concurrent differing values produce an explicit `conflicts`
entry and no current value. A resolving event names every conflicting head as a
parent and therefore causally dominates them. Timestamp, lexical author order,
or arrival order never silently resolves ambiguity.

`add` gives each set value an `(eventId, value)` tag. `remove` names the exact
ancestor add events it observed. A concurrent add survives. Tombstones use the
same rule: `restore` removes only the ancestor tombstone IDs it names, so an
unobserved concurrent tombstone continues to hide the object. History is never
erased.

## Moderation lineage

The first `decide` event is moderator-signed and binds its subject. An `appeal`
must be signed by the subject creator, name an ancestor `decide`/`resolve` as
`predecessor`, and descend from it. A moderator `resolve` names both that
predecessor and appeal as ancestors. Skipped, cross-object, or forged lineage is
rejected.

Concurrent differing active decisions never pick a quiet winner: the subject
is visibly `quarantined` with `moderationConflict`. Equal decisions coalesce.
Resolved `hide`, `quarantine`, and `allow` project to hidden, quarantined, and
visible respectively; the signed decision and appeal history remains readable
to authorized audit tools.

## Storage, migration, and recovery

The portable log format is one canonical envelope per NDJSON line with LF
record separators. Export sorts unique raw records by their raw SHA-256 digest.
Import verifies every line and recomputes state; it does not trust an exported
snapshot or silently normalize CRLF records.

Legacy `forkmesh-issue-v1`, `forkmesh-pull-v1`, comment, label, reaction,
review, milestone, project/board, notification, and moderation records migrate
through an importer-signed `create`/`decide` event. That event binds the exact
legacy record digest and records `valid`, `invalid`, or `unavailable` legacy
signature status. It never claims the legacy author made a new signature. The
original bytes stay beside the new log until retention policy permits archival.

Roll back readers before writers: stop emitting v1, keep accepting and
preserving raw envelopes, and project the prior snapshot format read-only. Do
not down-convert or delete v1 events because that loses causality. Recovery is
to restore policy plus NDJSON, run the independent verifier, and compare the
state digest. Corrupt lines remain quarantined while valid independent objects
continue folding.

Use the verifier locally:

```bash
python3 tools/verify_collaboration.py \
  --policy repository-collaboration-policy.json \
  --require-complete collaboration.ndjson
```

`tools/export_collaboration_log.py export --repository IDENTITY --signing-key
SEED` performs this import for a checkout's `forkmesh-issue-v1` records. It
writes `.forkmesh/collaboration/policy.json` and `issues.ndjson`, which can be
committed so a visitor verifies them from a plain clone. The digest binds the
exact record file bytes, and each record's legacy status is `valid` only when
every legacy event signature in it verifies.

The exporter carries its own copy of `issue_event_content` from
`app/src/events.py`, because that module needs the Worker's js bridge and a
stdlib tool cannot import it; `app/tests/test_export_collaboration_log.py` pins
the two byte-for-byte. A legacy `open` event is signed before the issue has a
number, so its signature may bind either 0 or the assigned number; every other
event binds the number. Signing uses `cryptography` when installed and falls
back to pure-Python RFC 8032. A record that v1 cannot represent, such as a
title over the 512-byte limit, is skipped and named in the export summary
rather than truncated, so the log never misstates an issue.

## Threat, abuse, privacy, and telemetry

The main threats are forged authorship, replay across repositories, malicious
clock/timestamp choice, key equivocation, reference retargeting, unauthorized
moderation, deletion races, and a relay omitting events. Signatures and domain
binding address forgery/replay; DAG validation and explicit conflicts address
ordering; role policy and lineage address moderation; observed tombstones
address deletion races. Omission requires peer exchange/availability receipts
and cannot be solved by a fold over an incomplete set.

Raw events can contain private issue text, notification recipients, moderation
notes, and relationship metadata. Private logs stay inside the repository's
authorization/encryption boundary. Telemetry exports counts only:
`received`, `uniqueRaw`, `signatureValid`, `accepted`, `pending`, `rejected`,
`duplicateDeliveries`, `equivocations`, `conflicts`, rejection reason, and
accepted family. It MUST NOT export bodies, object IDs, public keys, refs, or
raw signatures.

## Automated evidence and supported runtimes

`app/tests/test_collaboration_protocol.py` supplies the signed convergence
corpus, randomized permutations/replays, byte mutation fuzzing, adversarial
authorization/signature/sequence cases, all-family legacy migration,
rollback/recovery, telemetry, and Python↔WebCrypto parity. The dedicated
`collaboration-conformance.yml` workflow runs it with Python 3.12 and Node 24 on
Linux, macOS, and Windows and retains JUnit evidence. The same focused suite is
part of the core quality gate.

No network service, wall clock, or database is required. This is intentional:
an implementation passes only by deriving state from retained signed bytes.

pages.title: Pull request review threads across patchsets
pages.description: A review thread is pinned to a path, a side (old/new) and a line range of the diff the reviewer saw. When the pull is updated, lines shift or disappear. Threads therefore carry a…
pages.markdown:
# Pull request review threads across patchsets

A review thread is pinned to a path, a side (`old`/`new`) and a line range of
the diff the reviewer saw. When the pull is updated, lines shift or disappear.
Threads therefore carry a signed anchor so every client can show them on the
right lines or mark them explicitly as moved or outdated.

## The anchor

Line-anchored events (`line-comment`, `thread-comment`) may carry:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `patchset` | The head commit the reviewer's diff was cut against (empty for a portable patch-backed pull) |
| `anchorLines` | The exact text of the commented lines on that side, prefix stripped, newline-joined, at most 12 lines |

Both are signed: when present, the signed content appends
`NUL patchset NUL anchorLines` to the existing per-type content under the
unchanged `forkmesh-pull-comment-v1` label. Events without an anchor sign the
same bytes as before. On disk (`.forkmesh/pulls/<n>/NNNN-<type>.md`) they are
front-matter keys `patchset` and `anchorLinesB64` (base64url). Cross-language
vectors live in `desktop/tests/test_crypto.cpp` and `app/tests/test_crypto.py`.

## Placement

Desktop (`PullReviewModel.cpp`) and web (`06-repo-content.js`) apply the same
rule:

1. **Same patchset**: the thread is *current* at its lines.
2. **Text search**: otherwise, find `anchorLines` as consecutive lines on the
   same side, nearest the original line. Same line: *current*; elsewhere:
   *moved*; not found: *outdated*.
3. **Patchset only**: a different patchset with no anchor text is *outdated*.
   A diff with no named patchset keeps the thread *current* while the line
   exists.
4. **Legacy** (no anchor): painted where it says while the line exists,
   otherwise *outdated*.

Moved threads show a `Moved` badge and the original lines. Outdated threads are
never painted on a line; they are listed at the top of their file with an
`Outdated` badge. Applying a suggested change uses the current line and refuses
when the thread is outdated. Matching is exact on purpose: a thread is never
shown on code it did not discuss.

## Branch review threads

A branch without a pull request can be reviewed the same way, from the desktop
compare view or the phone apps. Branch threads use the same event types and
anchors and are stored in the `forkmesh/pulls` ledger branch under
`.forkmesh/branch-reviews/<first 24 hex of sha256(branch)>/` with a
`branch.md` naming the branch, so pull loaders never treat them as pulls.
Placement uses anchor text only, because a branch view can include
uncommitted changes.

Signature:
`forkmesh-branch-comment-v2\n<owner/name>\n<type>\n<branch>\n<author>\n<ts>\n<sha256 hex of contentForSigning>`.

Rendering only reads an existing ledger checkout; only posting a comment
creates it.

A phone cannot write Git, so it sends the signed event to
`POST /api/repo/<owner>/<name>/pulls` with `{"branch": "<name>", "event": {...}}`
and no `number`. The relay verifies the v2 signature and queues it in
`pull_inbox` with `number: 0`. The owner's desktop
(`PullStore::applyRemoteBranchEvent`) or a Go mirror (`writeBranchReviewItem`)
drains it into the ledger, skipping event ids already stored. Shared vectors
are pinned in `app/tests/test_branch_review_intake.py`,
`server/intake_test.go` and the iOS and Android test suites.

## Limitations

- The web compare page does not show branch review threads.
- The web places threads against the signed creation diff, so threads written
  against a later desktop head appear moved or outdated there.
- Whitespace-only edits and renames make a thread outdated.

pages.title: Release binary publishing
pages.description: Release binaries are never committed to git. A release is two things kept apart on purpose
pages.markdown:
# Release binary publishing

Release binaries are never committed to git. A release is two
things kept apart on purpose:

- **Metadata**: small, signed text committed to the repository and synced
  across the mesh like issues and pull requests.
- **Payloads**: the binary bytes, kept in a content-addressed store (CAS) on
  the node that serves the repository, and fetched by their SHA-256.

A mirror can carry the bytes, but it cannot change them without breaking the
signed hash, and git history never grows by the size of a build.

## Two kinds of release

**Repository releases.** Any repository can publish releases from the web or
the desktop. The manifest's canonical body is built by
`release_manifest_content` in `app/src/releases.py`: repository, tag, the
commit the tag pointed to (`tag_commit`), the commit embedded in the artifact
(`build_commit`, when present), and one line per asset (name, blob SHA-256,
size, content type, OS, architecture, label), sorted. The creator signs
`release_signing_message`:

```text
forkmesh-release-v1\n<repo>\n<tag>\n<author>\n<ts>\n<sha256 of the content>
```

with their Ed25519 identity; `verify_release_manifest` in `app/src/events.py`
checks it. Release name, notes and the prerelease flag are not signed, so they
can be edited without invalidating the release. Download counts are not
signed either.

**ForkMesh's own desktop releases.** Channels under
`.forkmesh/releases/<channel>/` (`latest`, `candidate-<version>`) hold
`SHASUMS256.txt`, `release.json` and `release.json.sig`: a raw 64-byte Ed25519
signature over the exact `release.json` bytes, made with the release publisher
key (not a user identity). `tools/forkmesh-release-publish.sh` writes them;
`www/public/install.sh` and the desktop updater verify them. Operating
instructions are in
[`.forkmesh/releases/README.md`](../../../.forkmesh/releases/README.md) and the
developer overview in [`docs/release/README.md`](../../../docs/release/README.md).

## The content-addressed store

Blob path, relative to the store root (`cas_blob_relpath` in
`app/src/releases.py`):

```text
sha256/<first two hex digits>/<full sha256>/data
```

The served store is `<bare repository>/forkmesh-releases/` on each mirror
(`server/bootstrap.go`, `server/gateway.go`). A local publish without
`--cas-dir` writes to `.forkmesh/release-blobs/`, which `.gitignore` excludes.

## Download

```text
GET /api/repo/<owner>/<repo>/releases/blob/sha256/<sha256>?filename=<asset name>
```

The route is matched in `app/src/urls.py`. The response is immutable and can
be cached forever at the edge; the App forwards it to a node holding the blob.
`filename` only sets the download name and never changes which bytes are
returned. Installers ask the repository recorded in the manifest (`repo`),
because only that node is guaranteed to hold the blob.

## Verification order

1. Authenticate the metadata: the release signature against a trust anchor
   (the publisher key built into `install.sh`, a local PEM, or a digest from
   an authenticated controller).
2. Check that the manifest binds `SHASUMS256.txt` (`checksums_sha256`).
3. Download the blob by hash and check its SHA-256 before installing or
   running it.

Nothing downloaded is executed to decide whether it is trustworthy.

## Related

- `app/src/releases.py`: tag and asset-name validation, CAS layout, canonical
  manifest, `SHASUMS256.txt` generation, semver ordering for `latest`, and the
  re-upload decision for an asset name.
- `app/tests/test_releases.py`

pages.description: Status: protocol version 1, candidate. The dependency-free reference resolver is app/src/trust_lists.py. The vectors in conformance/trust-lists/v1/vectors.json bind four…
pages.markdown:
# Scoped community trust lists

Status: protocol version 1, candidate. The dependency-free reference resolver
is `app/src/trust_lists.py`. The vectors in
`conformance/trust-lists/v1/vectors.json` bind four independent resolvers to
it byte for byte: the web client (`app/public/trust-lists.js`), the iOS client
(`native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Sources/FMAccount/TrustLists.swift`, tested by
`native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Tests/FMAccountTests/ConformanceTests.swift`), the
Android client
(`native/android/core/src/main/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/security/TrustLists.kt`,
tested by
`native/android/core/src/test/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/security/TrustListsCryptoTest.kt`),
and the desktop client (`desktop/src/TrustLists.cpp`). The user guide is
[Trust lists](../trust-lists.md).

## Goals and non-goals

A trust list is a signed statement that says, for example, "in the `forkmesh`
organization, these keys are security researchers whose advisories I stand
behind". People follow the lists they find useful. ForkMesh does not run a
global list, and no list is followed by default.

- **Reputation is scoped.** Every entry names one role and one repository,
  organization, or community. There is no wildcard or global scope. A follow,
  an include, or a delegation can only narrow scope, never widen it.
- **Nothing essential depends on a list.** Cloning, reading, identity,
  sign-in, pushing, and opening issues or pull requests never consult trust
  lists. A client with no follows behaves exactly as it does today. Lists
  inform ranking, review routing, badges, and moderation queues.
- **Disagreement stays visible.** When followed lists disagree, the result is
  `conflict`. Only the user's local override picks a side.
- **Compromise is recoverable locally.** Equivocation, a forked history, or
  a revocation cuts a list back to its last good version. The client shows
  the list as `recovered` instead of silently following the newest document.

## Documents

Documents are canonical JSON. Every string is printable ASCII other than `"`
and `\`. Object keys are sorted by code point, there is no whitespace, and
integers are at most 2^53−1 in magnitude, with no fractions, exponents, or
`-0`. A receiver accepts a document only when re-encoding its parse
reproduces the received bytes exactly. The restricted alphabet lets every
language write this encoding with a plain sorted-key writer. A raw document
is at most 262,144 UTF-8 bytes.

A document's identifier is `sha256:<hex SHA-256 of the raw bytes>`. Because
the raw bytes include the signature, two documents with the same meaning but
different signatures have different identifiers.

The signed message is the document's `schema` value, a newline, and the
canonical JSON of the document without its `signature` key. Signatures are
Ed25519 over those bytes. The rules of FM-SIG-001 in the
[protocol suite](../protocol/signatures-and-authentication.md#ed25519) apply.
Every resolver also rejects a scalar `S ≥ L` explicitly before calling a
platform verifier. It also rejects non-canonical key encodings (including
x = 0 with the sign bit set), the identity, and small-order and mixed-order
keys. Platform verifiers such as WebCrypto and OpenSSL do not, so the iOS and
Android resolvers use their own strict verifier (`Ed25519.verifyStrict`).
The `forged-weak-keys` vector carries signatures that pass lax verification
for each of those keys. Keys are 43-character and signatures 86-character
unpadded base64url, and both must round-trip.

A list is identified by issuer key and name, not by any single version:

```text
listId = "urn:forkmesh:trust-list:sha256:" ||
         hex(sha256("forkmesh-trust-list-id-v1\n" || issuer || "\n" || name))
```

### List version (`forkmesh-trust-list-v1`)

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `issuer` | Signing key of the list owner |
| `name` | Slug `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}` |
| `version` | Integer ≥ 1 |
| `previous` | `null` for version 1; otherwise the document identifier of version − 1 |
| `issuedAt`, `expiresAt` | Milliseconds; `expiresAt > issuedAt`; lifetime at most 400 days |
| `roles` | Sorted, non-empty set of `maintainer`, `moderator`, `mirror-operator`, `organization`, `reviewer`, `security-researcher` |
| `communities` | Sorted, non-empty set of at most 64 scopes, none covered by another |
| `revocationKeys` | Sorted set of at most 4 keys, not including `issuer`, that may revoke later versions |
| `entries` | At most 2,000 `{subject, role, scope, stance, note}` entries, strictly sorted by subject, role, scope |
| `edges` | At most 16 `{kind, issuer, name, roles, communities, expiresAt}` edges, strictly sorted by issuer, name |
| `signature` | By `issuer` |

An entry's `stance` is `trust` or `distrust`. Its `note` is at most 280
characters. Its subject is never the issuer. An entry's role must be one of
the list's roles, and its scope must be covered by the list's communities.

An edge whose `kind` is `include` composes another list and has
`expiresAt: null`. An edge whose `kind` is `delegate` grants another key
authority to publish entries for this list and carries an integer
`expiresAt`. Either way, the edge's roles must be a subset of the list's
roles, its communities must be covered by the list's communities, and it
cannot name its own list.

### Scopes

| Scope | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `repo:<owner>/<repository>` | That repository |
| `org:<owner>` | Itself and every `repo:<owner>/…` |
| `community:<slug>` | Itself |

Owners match `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,38}`. Repositories match
`[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,100}` other than `.` and `..`. The intersection of two
scope sets keeps each member of one set that the other set covers. It then
removes duplicates and any member covered by another member.

### Revocation (`forkmesh-trust-list-revocation-v1`)

`{list, issuer, name, fromVersion, revokedBy, revokedAt, reason, successor}`,
signed by `revokedBy`. `list` must equal the listId of `issuer` and `name`.
`reason` is `compromised`, `malicious`, `retired`, or `superseded`.
`successor` is `null` or `{issuer, name}` of a different list.

A revocation is authorized when `revokedBy` is the issuer, or when a verified
version of the list with `version < fromVersion` names `revokedBy` in
`revocationKeys`. A recovery key committed before a compromise can therefore
revoke everything the attacker publishes. An attacker who adds keys in a
malicious version cannot use them to revoke the versions before it.
Revocations have no expiry. Revocation is monotonic, so no document can undo
one.

### Appeal (`forkmesh-trust-list-appeal-v1`)

`{subject, list, version, role, scope, statement, issuedAt}`, signed by the
`subject` it concerns, with a statement of 1–1,000 characters. Nobody can
appeal on someone else's behalf.

## Verification order

A resolver rejects a document at the first failing step and records
`{documentId, code}`:

1. `too_large`; bracket nesting deeper than 8 outside strings, found by a
   scan before any parser runs, or unparseable JSON: `invalid_json`;
   `noncanonical`; a top level that is not an object, or a `schema` that is
   not a known string: `unsupported_schema`; wrong key set: `invalid_keys`.
2. List version: `invalid_issuer`, `invalid_name`, `invalid_version`,
   `invalid_previous`, `invalid_time`, `invalid_scope` (roles, then
   communities), `invalid_revocation_keys`. Then, entry by entry,
   `invalid_entry`, `entry_outside_scope`, `unsorted_entries`. Then, edge by
   edge, `invalid_edge`, `edge_outside_scope`, `unsorted_edges`. Last,
   `invalid_signature_encoding` and `invalid_signature`.
3. Revocation: `invalid_issuer`, `invalid_name`, `list_mismatch`,
   `invalid_version`, `invalid_revoker`, `invalid_time`, `invalid_reason`,
   `invalid_successor`, then the signature.
4. Appeal: `invalid_subject`, `invalid_list`, `invalid_version`,
   `invalid_scope`, `invalid_statement`, `invalid_time`, then the signature.
5. In context: a list version or appeal whose `issuedAt` is more than
   300,000 ms after the resolver's clock is rejected as `issued_in_future`,
   and an unauthorized revocation as `unauthorized_revoker`.

Duplicate raw documents are counted once.

## Version history

For each list, a resolver considers every verified version it holds:

- two different documents with the same `version` are an **equivocation** at
  that version;
- a document whose `previous` does not equal the identifier of the single
  held document for `version − 1` is a **history fork** at that version;
- an authorized revocation cuts at its `fromVersion`.

The cutoff is the lowest of these versions. The head is the highest held
version below the cutoff that has exactly one document. The list state is:

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `active` | A head exists, it has not expired, and nothing was cut |
| `recovered` | A head exists below a cutoff; `cutoffReasons` says why |
| `expired` | The head's `expiresAt` has passed; older versions are never revived |
| `revoked` | An authorized revocation left no usable version |
| `conflicted` | Equivocation or a fork left no usable version |
| `missing` | The list is followed or referenced, but no verified version is held |

Only `active` and `recovered` lists contribute entries and edges. A
revocation's `successor` is shown to the user and never followed
automatically. A compromised issuer key might have been used to revoke too,
so the user decides.

## Composition and merge

Local inputs are **follows**, `{issuer, name, roles, communities}` where a
`null` narrowing means the list's own scope, and **overrides**,
`{subject, role, scope, stance}` where the stance is `trust`, `distrust`, or
`ignore`. Neither is published or signed. They stay on the device. The client
that stores them validates them before resolving: keys and names use the
document field rules, and each override tuple appears at most once.
Resolvers do not re-validate local input.

1. Each follow starts a walk at its list, scoped to the intersection of the
   list's roles and communities with the follow's narrowing.
2. A walk admits each head entry whose role is in the walk's roles and whose
   scope is covered by the walk's communities.
3. A walk follows each edge. An expired delegation is skipped and counted.
   An edge back to a list already on the path is skipped as a cycle. An edge
   from a path that already holds 4 lists is skipped as depth-limited.
   Otherwise the child walk's scope is the intersection of the current scope,
   the edge's scope, and the child's own scope. The walk stops if that scope
   is empty.
4. Each `(subject, role, scope)` tuple collects at most one source per list,
   the one reached by the shortest path, with ties broken by the
   newline-joined path. Its `stance` is the shared stance of its sources,
   `conflict` when they differ, or `none` when only an override names it.
   `effective` is the override when present, otherwise the stance.
5. A verified appeal attaches to the tuple's assertion when one of that
   assertion's sources is the appealed list. The appeal is `resolved` when the
   list's head is newer than the appealed version and no longer distrusts the
   tuple, and `open` otherwise. Appeals that match no assertion are counted as
   unattached.

The resolution is canonical JSON with `lists` sorted by `listId`,
`assertions` by subject, role, and scope, `sources` by `listId`, `appeals` by
identifier, `rejected` by identifier and code, and `conflicts` by their
canonical JSON. `conflicts` holds `stance` conflicts, noting whether an
override resolved them, plus `equivocation` and `history_fork` records. The
result does not depend on the order of documents, follows, or overrides.

## Telemetry and privacy

`telemetry` holds counts only (documents, rejections by code, lists by state,
assertions, conflicts, overrides, appeals, skipped edges), never keys, list
names or follows. Follows and overrides never leave the device. Clients SHOULD
fetch the whole public bundle, or fetch through a mirror they operate, so a
relay does not learn which lists interest them. Entries name keys, not account
names.

## Threats

| Threat | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| Stolen issuer key publishes a malicious version | Recovery key revokes `fromVersion`; followers fall back to the last good version as `recovered` |
| Issuer shows different versions to different followers | Equivocation cuts below the disputed version once both copies meet |
| Rewritten history | `previous` digest chain; a fork cuts the list |
| A list claims global authority | No global scope; entries and edges must stay inside the list's own scope |
| Delegate or included list overreaches | Scope intersection at every hop; delegations expire |
| Attacker revokes with a key added in a malicious version | Only keys named in a version *before* `fromVersion` may revoke |
| Stolen issuer key revokes the whole list | Accepted as a denial of service; the owner publishes a successor under a new key and followers choose to follow it |
| Signature malleability and canonicalization tricks | Byte-exact canonical re-encoding, strict base64url, and explicit `S < L` |
| Resource exhaustion | Size, entry, edge, community, and path-depth limits |
| Silent winner between lists | `conflict` until the user overrides |
| Forged appeals | Appeals must be signed by their subject |

## Rollout

Version 1 is additive: no existing route, table or authorization decision reads
it, and follows and overrides are local, so removing the resolvers is a full
rollback. Any change in meaning needs a new schema string; changing the vectors
means regenerating them with `generate_vectors.py` and passing all four
resolvers. Publishing lists over relays and the authoring and follow UI are not
implemented yet.

pages.markdown:
# Daily interface validation

One contract covers the responsive web dashboard and the web content embedded by
the desktop and mobile shells. Numeric limits live in
[`daily-interface-budgets.json`](daily-interface-budgets.json); weakening one
uses the expiring waiver process in
[`definition-of-done.md`](definition-of-done.md).

## Automated check

`npm run test:daily-interface` drives the production dashboard in Chromium at
desktop and mobile viewports. It fails CI when startup, browse, search, diff
construction, navigation or feedback latency exceed their budgets, and verifies
keyboard navigation and focus handling, semantic landmarks, contrast in both
themes, 200% zoom reflow, 44 CSS-pixel coarse-pointer targets, reduced motion,
accessible diffs, and empty, error, offline and retry states.

Performance events stay in the page and carry only operation, duration, budget,
source class (`local` or `remote`) and pass/fail; no account, repository, route,
query or content.

```bash
cd app/browser_tests
npm ci
npx playwright install --with-deps --only-shell chromium
npm run test:daily-interface
```

`app/tests/test_daily_interface_contract.py` keeps the runtime constants,
workflow and quality-gate registry in sync.

What the check relies on:

- Focus outlines come from the shared `:where(...):focus-visible` rules in
  `app/public/dashboard/shell.html`: a 3px ring on buttons and links, and a
  1px primary outline on text fields (`docs/app/dashboard-components.md`).
  Those rules have no specificity, so Tailwind's `focus:outline-none` replaces
  them with a transparent outline. The repository filter no longer carries
  that class, and the check asserts its outline is solid and visible.
- Text on solid `primary` must reach 4.5:1 in both themes
  (`docs/app/dashboard-colors.md`).
- On a coarse pointer every button is at least 44px tall; the header's menu
  button also gets `min-width: 44px`, because its padding and icon only reach
  34px.
- `fetchJson` retries a 5xx twice (400 ms, then 1.5 s) before it gives up, so
  the offline test fails the catalog three times before the error state shows.
- Clone commands use the site the page is served from, not the catalog's
  `cloneUrl`, so the test compares them with the page origin.

## Release usability gate

Each public release candidate needs a consented usability study covering
keyboard-only, screen-reader, touch and pointer users, reported per access need.
Only aggregate duration, completion, error count and satisfaction are recorded.

| Task | Target time | Maximum user errors | Required completion |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Browse to and open a file | 45 seconds | 1 | 90% |
| Copy a clone command | 45 seconds | 1 | 90% |
| Find and open an issue | 60 seconds | 1 | 90% |
| Review a diff and submit feedback | 120 seconds | 2 | 85% |
| Inspect mirrors and recover from offline | 90 seconds | 2 | 85% |

## Rollback

The command palette and measurement trail keep no server state; rollback is the
previous static asset set. If the catalog fails to load, the page stays usable
and offers a retry that bypasses cached data.

pages.markdown:
# ForkMesh feature definition of done

A feature is complete when its code and the following evidence can be reviewed
together. The pull-request template has one section per item. The GitHub mirror's CI
(`python3 tools/quality_gate.py pr-evidence`) rejects a pull request with a
missing or placeholder section; on ForkMesh the reviewer checks it.

1. **Threat review.** Trust boundaries, sensitive inputs, authority changes,
   failure behaviour. Authorization, identity, custody and repository privacy
   fail closed when uncertain.
2. **Abuse and privacy review.** Data collected, visibility, retention,
   deletion, consent, moderation and abuse cases. Raw IP addresses, secrets,
   private repository existence and private agent data never become public
   observability data.
3. **Benchmark and budget evidence.** The applicable performance budget, or a
   reproducible measurement, or a reason there is no hot path.
4. **Regression tests.** Success, denied, malformed-input and privacy or
   authorization boundary cases, with the commands and results.
5. **Operational evidence.** Deployment, configuration, rollback, monitoring
   and recovery.

## Running the gates

```bash
python3 tools/quality_gate.py validate
python3 tools/quality_gate.py run --profile core
python3 tools/quality_gate.py run --profile release
```

`core` is the fast local and CI gate. `release` adds the real-browser World
suite (pinned Playwright and Chromium). Native Qt, iOS and Android suites are
required where their toolchains exist; a missing toolchain is reported, never
counted as a pass. Desktop changes must also build the `forkmesh` app target,
since CI only builds the test targets. The responsive daily-interface journey is
described in [`daily-interface-validation.md`](daily-interface-validation.md).

## Changing a budget

Budgets live in `quality-gates.json`. Tightening needs no exception. Removing a
budget or raising a maximum requires a waiver:

1. Add a JSON record under `www/docs/engineering/quality-gate-waivers/` named
   after the budget ID, with every field `quality-gates.json` lists, a risk
   review, a UTC expiry date and the approving reviewer.
2. Run `python3 tools/quality_gate.py compare --base-ref <sha>`; it rejects
   silent removals and increases.
3. Restore or tighten the budget before the waiver expires.

pages.markdown:
# Quality-gate waivers

This directory contains temporary, reviewed exceptions for a removed or
weakened performance budget. A waiver file is named `<budget-id>.json`; it must
contain every field required by `../quality-gates.json`, use an ISO-8601 UTC
expiry time, and explain the measured risk.

Do not add a waiver for a tighter budget.

pages.title: Chat encryption and public integrations
pages.description: All chat traffic uses an outer AES-256-GCM room cipher whose passphrase is derived from the controller's DATA_KEY. It protects the wire and retained storage from third parties…
pages.markdown:
# Chat encryption and public integrations

All chat traffic uses an outer AES-256-GCM room cipher whose passphrase is
derived from the controller's `DATA_KEY`. It protects the wire and retained
storage from third parties, not from the controller operator. On top of it each
conversation has one policy:

| Conversation | Content policy | Who can read it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| World `#general`, public `#` channel | Device-to-device encryption to every device in the room | Anyone who joins the room: guests, and the controller, which can join as a device |
| Private channel or direct message | Device-to-device encryption inside the room cipher | Only the members (the server checks who may join); a private channel's webhook and notice lines are also readable by the server |

Every person's message is sealed and signed by their device, in public rooms
too, so nobody can post, edit or delete as that person. That does not hide
public rooms from the server: they run the open policy, so any device that
joins gets the keys of the messages sealed after it arrived, and the
controller can join as a device. Public channels are controller-readable;
nothing private belongs there. Direct messages, private channels and Cove
invites never travel through a shared room; they use the server's direct and
private rooms, and clients drop such frames if they show up in a shared room.

Apps, webhooks and ForkMesh's own notices are posted unsealed by the server,
in public and private channels alike (never in direct messages), so the server
can read them; clients mark a webhook's line "server-visible". The server marks
each frame it injects, removes that mark from anything a client sends, and
clients show a marked frame as the app or webhook it names, never as a person.
An unmarked, unsealed frame is dropped.
A line a device posts for ForkBot shows as "forkbot · via" the person who
posted it. Making a channel public affects only new messages; making it
private rotates the room key and revokes its incoming webhooks.

Device-to-device encryption uses chat protocol v3 (October 2026), and direct
messages use v4, which adds a per-message ratchet. Every client (web, desktop,
iOS, Android) speaks only these; older v2 frames are ignored. The full
specifications are `docs/app/chat-protocol-v3.md` and
`docs/app/chat-protocol-v4.md` in the ForkMesh repository.

## Device keys

Each installation keeps two kinds of keys on the device (browser storage
wrapped by a non-extractable key where the browser supports it, the desktop
secure store, the iOS keychain, Android Keystore-wrapped storage):

- an **identity key** (Ed25519) for the life of the install, which signs
  everything the device sends;
- **prekeys**, each an X25519 key plus an ML-KEM-768 (post-quantum) key. A new
  prekey is made every 24 hours and its private half is deleted 8 days after it
  was made.

Private keys never leave the device.

## Bundles and new devices

A device announces itself in each room with a signed bundle: its identity key,
its newest prekey, the account it belongs to and the sender id it uses in that
room. Other devices check the signature before using it.

- In every room except direct messages the sender id is the device's own
  Ed25519 node key, and the bundle carries a second signature by that key. A
  bundle without it is dropped, and a key id already seen keeps its sender id,
  so one device cannot speak, edit or delete as another. Browsers keep a
  separate node key for a signed-out visitor and for each account, so a
  guest's messages cannot be linked to the account signed in later.
- The account name in a bundle is only a claim. Clients show it after the
  server confirms that the node key is bound to that account (each device binds
  its key at sign-in); otherwise the sender is shown as a guest.
- Edits, deletes, reactions, stickers and thread replies count only from
  sealed frames, and an edit or delete only from the message's author.

- Before v3 the server could add a key to a direct message and every client
  would start encrypting to it. Now, in a direct message, a bundle that names anyone other than the two people in the
  conversation is dropped, and a second device for an account that already
  has one is **held**: it receives nothing and its messages are not shown until
  you approve it. You see a line in the conversation and a banner with Approve
  and Block.
- Channels and Office rooms accept every validly signed device whose bundle
  is also signed by its node key.

## Sealed messages

For each message the sender picks a random content key and encrypts
the message with AES-256-GCM. For each approved device it then combines a fresh
X25519 exchange with an ML-KEM-768 encapsulation to that device's prekey,
derives a wrapping key with HKDF-SHA256, and wraps the content key. The whole
frame, including every wrapped key, is signed by the sender's identity key and
carries a counter and a timestamp.

A receiving device rejects a frame that:

- is not signed by an approved device;
- claims a sender id other than the one in that device's signed bundle;
- repeats a counter it has already accepted (the relay replaying a frame);
- was not wrapped for one of its kept prekeys.

Relay-held copies are kept for up to 7 days; prekeys live 8, so a message can
still be opened while it is waiting. After a prekey is deleted, nothing sealed
to it can be opened again, even with the device in hand.

## Direct messages: a key for every message

In a direct message each pair of devices runs a ratchet, like Signal's Double
Ratchet. The first message starts it with the same X25519 + ML-KEM-768 exchange
against the other device's prekey; after that every message has its own key,
derived from a chain that only moves forward, and the key is deleted as soon as
the message is opened. Each time the conversation changes direction, both
devices mix in a fresh X25519 exchange and a fresh ML-KEM-768 encapsulation.

- A device stolen today cannot open direct messages it had already received:
  their keys are gone.
- A device that was compromised recovers once the other person replies; against
  a quantum-capable attacker, once its prekey rotates (24 hours).
- A device never encrypts to itself; your own messages stay in your device's
  history, not in a copy the server holds for you.
- If a device loses its ratchet state, it asks the sender to start over and
  the sender re-sends what it still holds.

## Safety numbers

In a direct message, the encryption panel shows a 60-digit safety number and a
QR code. It covers every approved device of both people. Compare the digits
with the other person, or scan their code, then mark the conversation verified.
If an approved device is added or removed the number changes, the verified mark
is cleared and the conversation says so.

## Limits

- The controller still sees who talks to whom, when, and how much, and it can
  drop or delay frames.
- Channels approve every device that presents a valid bundle; only direct
  messages hold new devices. World and public channels are open rooms: anyone
  who joins can read what is said there from then on.
- In channels and Office rooms, forward secrecy is per prekey, not per
  message: a device compromised today exposes the channel messages sealed to
  the prekeys it still holds (up to 8 days). Channels keep this because the web
  reopens their history from the relay on every load.
- In direct messages, the messages sent before the other device first replies
  still rest on its prekey (up to 8 days); Signal adds one-time prekeys for
  these.
- A new device cannot read messages sent before it was approved.
- A modified web client served by a compromised host can read what it shows
  you, as with any web app.
- None of this has had an outside security audit yet.

## Compared with Signal

Direct messages now have per-message forward secrecy, as Signal does. Signal
is still ahead in one way: sealed sender hides who sent a message from Signal's
own server, while the ForkMesh server still knows which two accounts are in a
direct message. That is the next step. ForkMesh adds post-quantum key agreement
at the start of every session and on every ratchet step, a signature on every
frame, holds a new device of a contact until you approve it (Signal warns and
keeps sending), and lets nearby devices chat directly over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth
without a server.

## Implementations

Browser (`app/public/chat-seal.js`, `app/public/chat-mlkem.js`,
`app/public/chat-room-transport.js`, `app/public/chat-frame-auth.js`), desktop (`desktop/src/RoomSeal.{h,cpp}`),
iOS (`FMCrypto/RoomSeal.swift`) and Android (`crypto/RoomSeal.kt`) all open the
shared wire vectors in `conformance/chat/v3/vectors.json`,
`conformance/chat/v3/node-binding.json` and
`conformance/chat/v4/vectors.json`, so a change to key
derivation, signed strings, encoding or frame shape fails the cross-client
tests.

pages.description: A periodic review of every third-party component the repository resolves, in every ecosystem: publisher, maintenance history, known advisories and a score. The filterable report…
pages.markdown:
# Dependency security audit

A periodic review of every third-party component the repository resolves, in
every ecosystem: publisher, maintenance history, known advisories and a score.
The filterable report is at
**[the dependency audit report](/docs/dependency-audit/)**.

## Method

Package metadata comes from each ecosystem's registry (npm, PyPI, go.dev,
Gradle/Maven plugin indexes) and advisories from the OSV database, queried per
package and exact pinned version. Toolchains (Go, Kotlin, Android Gradle
Plugin) are audited alongside libraries, since a stale toolchain can carry
standard-library advisories even when every package is current.

## Scoring rubric

Each package starts at 100 and loses points for risk signals.
Grades: A ≥ 90, B 80–89, C 70–79, D 60–69, F below 60.

| Signal | Deduction |
| --- | --- |
| Open advisory matching the pinned version | −40 |
| Advisory in the package's history, pinned version not affected | −5 |
| Discontinued or deprecated | −30 |
| No verified publisher | −15 |
| Verified community publisher | −5 |
| No release in more than 24 / 12 months | −20 / −10 |
| Pinned version over 18 months old and a major version behind | −5 |
| Registry quality score below threshold, or analysis pending | −10 / −5 |
| Ships native code (plugin or FFI) | −5 |
| npm: fewer than two maintainers | −10 |

## Acting on findings

1. Open advisories on a pinned version or toolchain are fixed first: upgrade,
   rebuild and redeploy the affected component.
2. Packages that hold keys or secrets are kept on current major versions.
3. Stale packages and toolchains are upgraded in batches with the full test
   suite for the affected platform.
4. New dependencies in any ecosystem (including Swift packages and native
   Android Gradle dependencies) are added to the next audit.

pages.markdown:
# Organization roles and the authorization matrix

Every organization request is decided by one deny-by-default table,
`app/src/organization_rbac.py`. A role holds a capability only when the matrix
names it; unknown roles, empty roles and unlisted capabilities are refused for
everyone, owners included. The tables below are generated from that module and
checked against it by `app/tests/test_organization_rbac.py`.

## Roles

Strongest first.

| Role | Purpose | Repository permission on linked repositories |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `owner` | Runs the organization. The only role that can dissolve it or grant and revoke `owner`/`admin`. | `admin` |
| `admin` | Administers members, teams, linked repositories, integrations and bot tokens. Cannot promote anyone to `owner`/`admin` or demote them. | `admin` |
| `maintainer` | Ships code: may queue agents and manage bots it links, administers nothing. | `maintain`, a team grant can raise it to `admin` |
| `member` | Collaborates. | `read`, a team grant can raise it to `admin` |
| `auditor` | Read-only observer: sees the roster, agent work and internal surfaces, never writes, pushes or votes. | `read`, a team grant cannot raise it |
| `guest` | Outside collaborator: sees the public profile and only the repositories a team grants, read-only. Not an insider for world floors, office chat channels, task boards or succession votes. | none, a team grant raises it to `read` at most |

## Capabilities

`read` capabilities never change organization state; no `write` row lists
`auditor` or `guest`.

| Capability | Kind | owner | admin | maintainer | member | auditor | guest |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `organization.agents.queue` | write | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| `organization.agents.read` | read | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `organization.bots.link` | write | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| `organization.bots.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.chat.channels` | write | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| `organization.dissolve` | write | yes | no | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.fediverse.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.issues.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.members.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.pull_rules.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.read` | read | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `organization.repositories.import` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.repositories.link` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.roles.administer` | write | yes | no | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.roster.read` | read | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `organization.settings.write` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.succession.approve` | write | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| `organization.tasks.administer` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.teams.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.world.private` | read | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.world.restricted` | read | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |

## Role administration

- An `owner` may assign or remove any role.
- An `admin` may manage `maintainer`, `member`, `auditor` and `guest`
  accounts, but cannot grant `owner`/`admin` or change an account holding one.
- Other roles assign nothing.
- The last `owner` can never be removed or demoted.

Denied writes are recorded in the sensitive-action audit log with a reason
(`insufficient_role`, `owner_role_required`, `last_owner`).

## Enforcement points

- Organization settings, members, teams, linked repositories, integrations,
  bot tokens and repository imports.
- `_org_permission`, used by the Git push gate and every repository-permission
  check: the role's baseline, raised by team grants up to the role's ceiling.
- A linked repository's Settings tab and every endpoint behind it (About,
  features, federation switches, webhooks, provider mirror, Actions secrets,
  logo review, delete) need repository permission `admin`, so `owner` and
  `admin` hold it and `maintainer` does not unless a team grants `admin`; the
  account that stores the repository keeps it too
  (`docs/app/repo-settings-access.md` in the source tree).
- World building access, office chat channels, task boards and succession
  votes, which enumerate the insider roles in SQL.
- Notes shared with the organization, organization package state
  (`/api/plugins/<org>` and the package list), installing or requesting an
  app for the organization, and slash commands from its app installs. These
  are insider surfaces too, so a guest gets none of them. An auditor reads an
  organization-shared note but never edits it, and cannot install apps.

Roles are stored as plain text in `org_members.role`; a build that does not
know a role treats it as no membership.

pages.title: Private repository confidentiality boundary
pages.description: The leakage and recovery contract for private repositories.
pages.markdown:
# Private repository confidentiality boundary

The leakage and recovery contract for private repositories.

## Protected data

Repository objects and refs, artifacts, repository and organization names,
device labels, discussions, issues, pull requests and reviews, agent prompts
and transcripts, notifications, security findings, media, and any search terms
or indexes derived from them.

Two confidentiality boundaries apply:

- **Repository objects** are sealed on an authorized device as
  `forkmesh.private-replica` ciphertext (fresh AES-256-GCM content key per
  update, wrapped to X25519 and ML-KEM-768 recipients). Storage and replication
  operators hold no recipient key and learn neither identity nor contents.
- **Relay collaboration rows** are AES-256-GCM encrypted under the instance
  `DATA_KEY`, with a separately derived HMAC blind index for equality lookups.
  Owner-agent payloads and private rooms add recipient encryption on top. An
  operator holding the live service and `DATA_KEY` is inside this boundary; a
  database, log or backup operator without it is not.

A missing recipient key never falls back to plaintext.

## Metadata envelope

At-rest inspection may reveal only random identifiers, keyed blind indexes,
counts, ciphertext sizes, coarse status values, timestamps, digests, key epochs,
algorithm and public-key identifiers, and a private flag. These leak existence,
activity volume and equality within one key lifetime, but never names, paths,
labels, message text, Git refs or object IDs. Public-mirror history tables hold
no rows for private repositories.

Plaintext still exists in authorized memory, exported working copies and
recipients' own copies; use disk encryption alongside ForkMesh keys.

## Key lifecycle

Each repository update or recipient change creates a new content key and
advances `keyEpoch` atomically. To revoke a device or collaborator: remove the
recipient, reseal to the fresh owner-signed recipient set, publish the new
epoch, and verify the removed key cannot open it and an older epoch cannot
overwrite it. Revocation cannot erase copies already held. Keep at least two
owner recipients; organizations may escrow a recipient key in their own KMS and
enroll only its public half.

## Backup and keyless inspection

Back up `.fm-private` files, the encrypted database export, configuration and
the identity recovery kit, never plaintext checkouts or the raw `DATA_KEY`
alongside ciphertext. Restore ciphertext and schema together.

```bash
python tools/audit_private_surfaces.py backup.sqlite3 \
  --replica-root /read-only/private-replicas \
  --output artifacts/private-surface-audit.json
```

The audit takes no key and checks column declarations, blind-index shape,
payload and replica framing, digests and epoch monotonicity. Exit `0` passes,
`1` is a confidentiality finding, `2` is an input failure; an undeclared column
or incomplete coverage fails closed.

## GA evidence

Commercial general availability requires, per release candidate: private-surface
CI on Linux, macOS and Windows; keyless inspection of primary, backup, log and
replica data; revocation, rotation and recovery drills including failure paths;
content-free telemetry; and an independent cryptographic and tenant-isolation
review. Any unresolved critical or high finding, plaintext finding or missing
review blocks GA.
